articles.fullText:
The first clinical trial of an Ebola vaccine in the outbreak gripping the Democratic Republic of the Congo has begun, the head of the World Health Organisation (WHO) said.

The DR Congo's worst-ever Ebola outbreak has passed the 9,700-case mark, with the number of deaths exceeding 4,600.

Among the many challenges facing the response is the lack of any approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the epidemic.

Ervebo, a vaccine approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will be put through a full-scale human trial in the DRC to see if it offers any cross-protection against Bundibugyo.

"Science gives us hope. Today, in Bunia DRC, the first participants were vaccinated in a new Ebola vaccine trial called Tumaini, which means 'hope' in Swahili," WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on X on Friday.

"This trial will help us understand whether any of the vaccine candidates designed for Bundibugyo virus work.

"In the meantime, the existing Everbo vaccine [licensed for use in preventing other Ebola virus disease] will be tested.

"WHO is supporting this DRC-led effort to find answers and save lives."

The so-called Tumaini trial in the DRC – a single trial framework that can test the safety and efficacy of multiple vaccines – should also eventually incorporate two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which are moving through earlier-stage, smaller-scale clinical trials.

One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab being developed by the University of Oxford; the other, by the US-based Moderna group, uses mRNA technology. (AFP)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Suspect held over large fire at Hitler's Eagle's Nest
articles.excerpt: German police on Saturday said they had detained a suspect following a fire at Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, known as the Eagle's Nest, in the state of Bavaria. "A suspicious person was taken into temporary custody," police said, following an earlier statement which said…
articles.fullText:
German police on Saturday said they had detained a suspect following a fire at Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, known as the Eagle's Nest, in the state of Bavaria.

"A suspicious person was taken into temporary custody," police said, following an earlier statement which said firefighters had found the building "completely ablaze".

The site once housed the Nazi leader's heavily fortified country residence where he relaxed with his companion Eva Braun and wrote part of his book "Mein Kampf".

Emergency services arrived on site at 9.52pm on Friday and found a large fire, the Upper Bavaria South police headquarters said.

Police spokeswoman Lisa Maier said firefighters were struggling to extinguish the blaze due to its remote location, at an altitude of 1,834 metres.

"The criminal police investigation is ongoing," she said. (AFP)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Forest out of Premiership relegation woods – for now
articles.excerpt: Nottingham Forest have climbed out of the Premier League relegation zone with a 1-1 draw away to Ipswich. The result could have been so much better for the visitors, with Forest missing several chances at Portman Road as a defensive error gifted Ipswich their equaliser. Oliver…
articles.fullText:
Nottingham Forest have climbed out of the Premier League relegation zone with a 1-1 draw away to Ipswich.

The result could have been so much better for the visitors, with Forest missing several chances at Portman Road as a defensive error gifted Ipswich their equaliser.

Oliver Glasner's men were the dominant side for much of the game and Forest deservedly went ahead in the 13th minute when Neco Williams turned in Daniel Munoz's right-wing cross at the back post for his first Forest goal since April.

The returning Morgan Gibbs-White had an effort saved by the toe of Ipswich goalkeeper Christian Walton before Leif Davis hacked the ball off the line.

Having been in control, Forest were undone in the 41st minute when a dawdling Nikola Milenkovic produced a backpass that was too short, with Julio Enciso seizing on the loose ball to slot past Forest keeper Matz Sels.

Forest thought they had a penalty early in the second half when midfielder James McAtee was brought down by Issa Diop.

Referee Thomas Bramall initially waved play on, but the VAR recommended an on-field review for a red card for the denial of a goalscoring opportunity.

After reviewing the footage, Bramall decided to award a yellow card and a free-kick, explaining McAtee "had knocked the ball to the right side of the goal".

An energised Forest then missed several chances as they went in search of what would have been just their second league win of the season following a poor start to the campaign under former Crystal Palace manager Glasner.

The unmarked Murillo headed a corner wide, Dan Ndoye had an effort cleared off the line and former Ipswich striker Liam Delap headed over from six yards and whipped a low shot just wide.

The point moved Forest above Coventry and Tottenham into 16th place on six points, although they could yet end the weekend back in the bottom three. Ipswich are ninth. (AFP)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Trump lifts some Canada tariffs ahead of midterms
articles.excerpt: With an incumbent Maine US senator from his own party locked in a tight reelection battle, US President Donald Trump signed an order on Friday to remove 50 percent tariffs on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products in a move that could benefit companies from the…
articles.fullText:
With an incumbent Maine US senator from his own party locked in a tight reelection battle, US President Donald Trump signed an order on Friday to remove 50 percent tariffs on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products in a move that could benefit companies from the northern state.

The Republican president's hefty tariffs on Canada have caused friction with the US neighbour to the north while creating problems for American businesses in Maine and other states that rely on certain Canadian goods.

With the November 3 US midterm elections looming and Republicans fighting to retain control of both houses of Congress, Senator Susan Collins had urged the White House to address tariffs on products affecting companies and farmers in Maine, a state that borders Canada.

Trump's order exempted plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and packing crates and boxes, as well as fresh and dried seaweed, the White House said.

The changes take effect on October 30, four days before the election.

Trump added a number of Canadian products to the 50 percent tariff list to offset the tariff relief provided in his order, including carpets, paints, waste, shampoos, cocoa powder, wooden coffins, ice cream sticks, air-conditioning machines, chest freezers, archery equipment and canoes.

Collins said the relief would aid Maine's blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed producers.

"These producers are a vital part of our state's economy and support our rural and coastal communities," Collins said.

"Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialised equipment, packaging materials and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense."

Democrat Troy Jackson is seeking to oust Collins in a race that polls indicate is very close.

The two sparred over tariffs at an October 6 debate.

"Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers," Jackson said on Friday after Trump's action.

"Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire."

Collins did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Jackson's remarks.

Trump in August imposed 50 percent tariffs on US$20 billion of Canadian imports, which took effect after talks between the two countries collapsed.

Canada retaliated in September with tariffs ranging from 15 percent to 50 percent on US$20 billion of American goods.

Canada and the United States have been in a standoff over the tariffs since Trump imposed them.

Trump asserted on Friday that Canada is working on a deal.

Republican candidates in northern US border states most affected by the tariffs, including Maine and Michigan, are trying to strike a balance between appealing to Trump's conservative base and winning over independent voters.

In a statement concerning Trump's action on Friday, White House spokesperson Matthew Middleton said the president "continues to address Canada's discriminatory treatment of US commerce" and that the new moves are "further refining the scope" of the previously announced tariffs.

Dominic LeBlanc, Canada's minister responsible for trade with the US, said Ottawa was assessing Trump's latest tariff change.

"Canada stands ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada's interests," LeBlanc said in a statement.

The economies of Michigan and Maine have long been intertwined with that of Canada, covering everything from auto parts to lumber to fruit-picking equipment.

Republicans may need to win closely contested Senate races in both states in order to maintain their slim majority in the chamber.

"Trump's desperate, 11th-hour attempt to save Susan Collins' political career is an admission that American voters are rejecting his toxic tariff policies," Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, said in a statement on Friday.

"No one will forget how Trump raised prices on thousands of products American families need by slapping trade taxes on goods from around the world."

Michigan US Senate candidate Mike Rogers, a Republican who previously called for ending the trade war with Canada, praised Trump for imposing tariffs on Canadian trash.

"If you’re going to be putting tariffs on anything from Canada, it ought to be the damn trash they’ve been dumping in our state for decades," Rogers said.

Trump's threat in September to block Canadian jet maker Bombardier from the US market became a political issue in Kansas, where the company employs 1,500 workers in Wichita.

Trump dropped the threatened ban this week after calls from Kansas lawmakers including Republican Senator Roger Marshall, who is also locked in a tough reelection race. (Reuters)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Trump orders lawsuit to stop Alaska result if GOP lose
articles.excerpt: US President Donald Trump on Friday said he ordered a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to prevent certification of Alaska's Senate election result if the Republican incumbent loses — ramping up questions over whether he will accept defeat in the midterms. "I'm the one that…
articles.fullText:
US President Donald Trump on Friday said he ordered a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to prevent certification of Alaska's Senate election result if the Republican incumbent loses — ramping up questions over whether he will accept defeat in the midterms.

"I'm the one that said, 'Do it,'" Trump announced during a trip to Florida, where he is due to cast his own early ballot for the November 3 election to decide control of Congress — currently in Republican hands.

The extraordinary intervention by a president to launch a preemptive challenge against a possible election result casts a new shadow over the midterms.

Trump — who tried to overthrow the 2020 presidential election after he lost to Democrat Joe Biden — has repeatedly questioned the validity of the upcoming election in which Democrats are forecasted to make big gains.

If Democrats win the House of Representatives, as widely expected, they would be able to exert the first real brake on Trump's unprecedented exercise of power since he secured his second term two years ago.

Democrats also have an outside chance of winning the Senate if they can flip a handful of Republican-held seats, including in Alaska, where incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan faces Democrat Mary Peltola.

She called the lawsuit "corruption" in a post on X.

In its lawsuit, filed Thursday, the US Justice Department alleged that the presence on the Alaska ballot of a minor additional candidate named Dan J. Sullivan Jr. is part of a deliberate ploy to confuse voters and harm the Republican incumbent's chances.

"The sole purpose of his candidacy is to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan," the lawsuit said.

Democrats and Sullivan Jr himself, a registered Republican, have denied this.

The lawsuit asks for certification of a Democratic win to be held up pending investigation if the Republican incumbent's losing margin is smaller than the votes won by his namesake.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, who has repeatedly broken Washington norms about keeping political distance from the White House, said on Thursday that the Justice Department was not preparing to interfere in the midterms.

But he refused to rule out what he called a "doomsday scenario."

"To say that there's no circumstances that we would ever do that. Of course, I'm not going to say that."

Democrats have accused the Trump administration of seeking ways to steer the results of the November vote by trying to expand federal government control over state-run elections and by repeatedly questioning the integrity of results.

Trump won Alaska by 13 percentage points in his 2024 comeback election.

But amid growing discontent with Republicans and Trump nationwide, Peltola, a former tribal judge and Alaska Native, is running a strong race.

Alaska is a vast state with a population of just 740,000.

Legal analyst Derek Muller described the Department of Justice's case as "absurdly thin" and unlikely to prevail in court.

"There's essentially no likelihood of success," Muller wrote on the Election Law Blog.

Sullivan Jr was briefly ejected from the ballot this summer, but he was reinstated by an Alaskan lower court — a decision affirmed by the state's supreme court. (AFP)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Rescuers search for seven in Nairobi building collapse
articles.excerpt: Rescuers were searching for seven people feared trapped after a multi-storey building under construction collapsed in Kenya's capital on Friday, the interior minister said. Videos shared online showed a dramatic crash and huge clouds of dust as the 16-storey building came down…
articles.fullText:
Rescuers were searching for seven people feared trapped after a multi-storey building under construction collapsed in Kenya's capital on Friday, the interior minister said.

Videos shared online showed a dramatic crash and huge clouds of dust as the 16-storey building came down in the densely populated business and residential area of Eastleigh.

The building lay in a pile of rubble as search and rescue teams arrived on the scene and struggled to start accessing the site which was jammed between other high-rise buildings.

"Eleven shops on the ground floor and in the basement were occupied at the time of the collapse. Seven people have been reported missing," Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen posted on X late Friday.

Murkomen said 66 of the 67 people working on the site had escaped unharmed, while one was injured.

Earlier, police said they had already rescued one woman from the rubble, and could hear the voice of another.

"The contractors and the engineers are supposed to ensure that the works are followed by professionals. But most are not," Bibiye Mahmoud, president of the Institution of Engineering Technology of Kenya, told AFP at the scene.

"This is why we are seeing these catastrophes... There is no accountability," she added.

Kenya's National Building Inspectorate report found that 87 percent of buildings audited nationwide last year failed to meet standards or lacked the required approvals.

"Our concern is to save lives," Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja told reporters, adding: "This building has no occupation certificate... this has potentially cost lives."

An occupation certificate is essentially the authority's formal sign-off that a building is safe and legally fit to be occupied.

John Ogallo, vice-president of the Institution of Engineers of Kenya, who was also at the site, said there were warning signs about the building.

"People here are saying distresses were observed, like cracks," before it collapsed, he told reporters.

If you build with the wrong materials, "it becomes a time bomb," he added.

Nairobi is undergoing a rapid construction boom, with high-rise buildings springing up across the city, particularly in Eastleigh which is known for its busy market areas and as a hub for the Somali community.

The number of buildings completed annually in Nairobi rose from 20,025 in 2022 to 25,090 last year, according to its statistics bureau, as east Africa's leading business hub sucks in people from rural areas and neighbouring countries.

Local media reported looting immediately after the collapse, which happened around lunchtime.

AFP saw police use tear gas to disperse crowds gathering near the site.

There were 86 building collapses between 2009 and 2019 in Nairobi, killing an estimated 200 people, according to a report by the Kenya Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis.

Corruption has allowed contractors to cut corners or bypass regulations.

Five people were killed when a six-storey building collapsed in a town on the outskirts of Nairobi in September 2022.

In April 2016, 49 people died when a six-floor apartment building crumbled in the northeast of the capital after days of heavy rain caused floods and landslides. (AFP)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: US stocks finish down; all eyes on Fed, oil prices
articles.excerpt: US markets closed lower on Friday, with investors concerned by rising oil prices, and also looking ahead to a Federal Reserve interest rate policy meeting. The Nasdaq Composite posted a slim loss a day after suffering its biggest one-day drop since June, as concerns flared over…
articles.fullText:
US markets closed lower on Friday, with investors concerned by rising oil prices, and also looking ahead to a Federal Reserve interest rate policy meeting.

The Nasdaq Composite posted a slim loss a day after suffering its biggest one-day drop since June, as concerns flared over financing costs to support heavy AI investment spending.

Next week, about one-third of S&P 500 companies report quarterly results, including Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, three AI hyperscalers.

"There is still fallout from the questioning of the AI trade," said Kristina Hooper, chief market strategist at Man Group.

"There's certainly the potential that we see less invested in an AI data centre build-out next year than has been projected. So I certainly think that's giving pause."

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 652.82 points, or 1.23 percent, to 52,215.16; the S&P 500 lost 39.75 points, or 0.52 percent, to 7,623.68 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 53.52 points, or 0.21 percent, to 25,955.34.

Telecommunications stocks fell, weighing on the communication services sector, after a report that SpaceX was seeking thousands of cell sites for a fourth wireless carrier.

The energy sector rose 2.5 percent, hitting a record high.

Brent crude hit its highest level since late April, after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concern over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East.

American Express shares fell 3.7 percent, weighing on the Dow.

The company raised its profit forecast as it also announced plans to eliminate five percent of its workforce.

Data from the University of Michigan showed US consumer sentiment edged down near a record low in October, as rising prices because of the Middle East conflict soured households' views of the economy.

Market focus remains on the earnings season, with robust corporate profit growth underpinning gains for major equity indexes this year.

The Fed is expected to keep interest rates steady when it gives its policy statement on Wednesday, but investors will be eager for clues about whether the US central bank will hike rates at its December meeting.

Wall Street is also increasingly focused on the November 3 midterm elections, which will decide control of the US Congress. (Reuters)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Live K-pop show makes South Korea more real to former North Korean arts troupe singer
articles.excerpt: “I really am in the South now,” said Cho Mi-young - at her first K-pop show - 22 years after fleeing North Korea
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Korean .
A white tiger entered the courtyard outside the National Museum in Seoul. He mugged for the camera and darted up the steps. At the top were the six members of BOYNEXTDOOR, wearing quasi-traditional outfits that mixed elements of hanbok with modern formal wear and a tinge of “bad boy” biker gear.
As they danced in unison and sang the opening lines of their hit single “Animal,” the crowd went wild.
Sitting in the audience was Cho Mi-young – born in Chongjin, North Korea – who arrived with her family in the South in 2004.
Mi-young can’t contain herself. “You’re so amazing!” she cries out, as the monitors show the young men dominating the courtyard with their precise dance moves.
Cho is in the audience at an episode of KBS Music Bank, a Friday night K-pop showcase program with all the latest acts. It has been the start of the K-pop weekend for most of its 28-year runtime. Surprisingly, it’s her first time ever seeing a live K-pop performance in person after 22 years in the South.
Tickets to studio tapings of KBS Music Bank are hard to come by. Fans either have to know someone, know someone who knows someone, or enter the ticket lottery. The episode she’s watching on Oct. 16 is special - it’s a live broadcast and the biggest boy bands, girl bands, and boy-girl bands are plying their craft on an outdoor stage on the grounds of the National Museum of Korea, which the show’s special intro vignette called the “beating heart of Korean culture.”
When the opening act was finished, the show’s hosts began introducing this week’s lineup, as Cho and the rest of the audience settled in. Many more K-pop groups and solo artists would take the stage in front of them on a night they would likely all remember forever.
“I’ve seen it a lot on TV, but today is the first time I’ve seen it with my own eyes,” Cho told Radio Free Asia. “Seeing such beautiful and handsome people dancing and singing right in front of me, moving like that, is absolutely mesmerizing.”
Cho is no stranger to music, or to the stage. In North Korea she had been a vocalist for a state-run provincial arts troupe. After settling in the South, Cho was a fixture in Seoul’s burgeoning musical theater scene and she toured as an accordion player. She later transitioned into broadcasting, at one point even co-hosting the RFA Korean webseries “ Northboy Northgirl .”
At present, she runs a content production company and maintains an active presence both online and in traditional media.
Cho Mi-young watches a live broadcast of KBS Music Bank at the National Museum of Korea in Seoul, Oct. 16, 2026.
(RFA) But today, she’s just a fangirl in a sea of other diehards, most of whom are screaming the names of the idols on stage.
Music in isolation
On the night of her first live K-pop concert, Cho reminisced about how she first encountered South Korean music in North Korea. At the time, she didn’t have access to what most would describe as K-pop today; instead she took in a lot of trot – a unique South Korean genre that mixes Western foxtrot dance rhythms with pentatonic minor scale melodies. Most young South Koreans consider trot to be music their grandparents like.
But after arriving in the South, she became a huge fan of South Korean love ballads, much slower than the catchiest K-pop numbers, but thicker in emotion. Music occupied much of her daily life in the South early on, as she scanned the radio for something new to listen to.
Today’s performances on the Music Bank stage were a far cry from her own back in North Korea. For one, everyone on stage just seems happy to be there, she said.
“When I performed in North Korea, I was always stiff,” she said. “When we were on stage, we performed with the mindset of conveying the Party’s voice, so I don’t think I ever had the thought that we were actually enjoying our own music.”
Several more musical acts came and went and then the undistorted electric guitar of indie rock band Jannabi’s Kim Do-hyung echoed through the air as vocalist Choi Jung-hoon sang the first few lyrics of “Thoughts on an Autumn Night.”
“Even on that distant shining star up there… love must be alive singing its song.”
The song struck a chord with Cho. Performed by just one singer and one guitarist it was a bit of a shift from the rest of the evening’s heavily choreographed bangers.
“The lyrical melody seems to have a bit of North Korean sensibility to it.”
She sat there, transfixed by Jannabi’s intimate, scaled down performance on the stage and quietly sang along.
“I really am in the South now”
When it was all over, Cho talked about her experience on the show, but it wasn’t only the dazzle of the K-pop acts that caught her eye. She was also amazed by the devoted fans, who sang along with every lyric from memory and chanted in pre-arranged cheers in unison. She thought back to how strange that seemed when she first arrived.
“I didn’t understand it in the past. But as I’ve lived here longer, I’ve come to understand the fans and their pre-prepared chants,” she said. “I think maybe next time, I might enjoy it even more if I learned those.”
The best performance of the evening, according to Cho, was by a co-ed group called AllDay Project. She thought they looked cool in their all-black outfits, some in furs, others in biker leather – almost like warriors.
But as an artist, Cho’s thoughts naturally turned to the massive effort that must have gone on behind the scenes. The meticulous choreography alone must take many months of practice, she said.
She recalled how she herself had put in a lot of effort as a singer back in North Korea.
“Even in North Korea, artists are trained very strictly in a Spartan manner,” she said. “In terms of the sheer volume of training, it might be difficult to see a significant difference between the North and South.”
But she noted that the payoff in the South is individual success, unlike the North, where it would merely advance the goals of the state.
She said the whole evening was surreal. Back when she was in North Korea, she could maybe catch glimpses of what the music scene in the South was like, but she could never actually see it. Now she finally has seen it in person, “it sinks in that I really am in the South now.”
Cho said that she thinks any North Korean escapee would probably feel the same way.
“The emotion felt in the live setting is completely different from listening to a recording,” she said. “I think many escapees would finally feel they truly have arrived in South Korea when they go to the venue, see the singer in person, and listen to the songs live.”
Edited by Yi Yongin in Korean and Eugene Whong in English.

articles.title: China closes 3 Tibetan schools in 3 months; threatens language, cultural preservation
articles.excerpt: Shutting schools in Golog region, Qinghai province, comes three months after "ethnic unity law" enacted on July 1.
articles.fullText:
Chinese authorities have shut down three Tibetan schools in the Golog region of Qinghai province in recent months, leaving the fate of students and teachers unclear, according to sources inside Tibet.
The closures of Gangjong Grassland Girls’ School, Jasag Village Primary School and Golog Tadra Orphan School have raised concerns among Tibetans about the future of education that incorporates their language, cultural traditions and community life.
Tibetan sources who spoke to Radio Free Asia linked the closures to the Chinese government’s education policies and its promotion of the Ethnic Unity and Progress Law , which took effect on July 1, 2026. They said the shutdowns could further limit opportunities for Tibetan children to learn their mother tongue and cultural traditions.
The Chinese government has cited the high altitude of Golog and shortages of teachers and educational resources as reasons for establishing schools outside the region, saying the move would improve education. It remains unclear where students from the three closed schools will continue their studies.
Education department declines to comment
RFA contacted the education department of the Golog Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture by phone to seek details about the closures.
“We don’t know the details,” the person told RFA, saying the initial work had been carried out by the Machen County administration and that the county’s education department was responsible for the matter.
RFA also contacted the Machen County Education Department, which said it had “no authority to respond.”
Unclear future for students
Gangjong Grassland Girls’ School in Ragya Township, Machen County, was closed on Aug. 28, according to a source in Tibet who spoke to RFA on condition of anonymity for security reasons.
The school had about 450 students and 60 teachers at the time of its closure, the source said. The current situation of the students remains unclear.
Gangjong Grassland Girls’ School in an undated photo.
(Citizen photo) The source said the school had been made a government-affiliated institution, with its curriculum following the Chinese government’s education system while retaining some Tibetan-language instruction.
“Currently, the schools in the Golog region are conducting a strong patriotic reeducation campaign,” the source said, adding that Tibetans were afraid to share information because of government restrictions.
Jasag Village Primary School, which was established in 1995 with funds raised by local nomadic families and renamed Ragya Township Residential School No. 2 in 2008, was shut down in September, according to information obtained by RFA. Another source in Tibet told RFA that the situation of its students and teachers remained unclear.
“The Golog Education Department has put considerable pressure on the school’s teachers and shut down the school without providing any clear explanation,” the source said.
Golog Tadra Orphanage School was ordered to close this month, according to information obtained by RFA. Founded in 2005, it provided education and support to Tibetan orphans and disadvantaged children for two decades.
At an event marking the school’s 20th anniversary in 2025, principal Thupten Nyima of the Golog Tadra Orphan School, which provides K-12 education, said it was training more than 1,000 students. Some graduates had gone on to work in government positions and as teachers, he said.
Nyima addressed students and teachers in a recent video posted to social media, saying, “Don’t be sad, students and teachers. If we are bound by karma and fate, all the teachers and students gathered here will sing a song of joy together.”
It is unclear if Nyima’s remarks were made around the time the school was ordered to close.
Critics warn of cultural impact
Dr. Gyal Lo, a Tibetan educational sociologist, said the closures marked a significant change in the Chinese government’s education policy in Tibet.
“The Chinese government sees schools where Tibetans can organize themselves to learn and teach their own culture as a thorn in its side. That is why these schools are being abolished,” he told RFA.
“After Xi Jinping visited Qinghai, the school established by Jigme Gyaltsen was closed , and a new secondary school was built in the eastern part of Ziling,” he said.
Gyal Lo said the closures could distance children from Tibetan traditions and customs practiced in their communities and place them in state-run boarding schools where Chinese is the language of instruction.
“The first impact of the Chinese government’s school closures is that children are distanced from the Tibetan traditions and customs practiced in their homeland. Secondly, when these children enter state-run boarding schools, the entire curriculum is taught in Chinese and is under the government’s control,” he said.
He argued that the policies could affect the transmission of Tibetan identity across generations.
“The aim is to turn the entire Tibetan people into Chinese. This is not limited to a small area; it is a plan with far-reaching consequences,” Gyal Lo told RFA. “The ultimate goal is to turn the younger generation of Tibetans into Chinese through different methods and policies implemented in different regions.”
He also emphasized the role of families in preserving the Tibetan language.
“According to language education theory, a language cannot be passed on to the next generation without being taught within the family. The foundation for preserving the mother tongue and passing it on to the next generation must be laid at home,” he said.
Tenzin Lekshey, spokesperson for the Central Tibetan Administration in Dharamsala, India, said Tibetan schools and monasteries played an important role in preserving the community’s language, culture, traditions and identity.
“The Chinese government is doing all this out of fear. Tibetan schools and monasteries established inside Tibet aim to preserve and protect the rich Tibetan language, culture, traditions and identity. But the Chinese government views these institutions as a hindrance rather than a benefit,” he told RFA.
Ragya Geshe Lobsang Palden, a former political prisoner, said the new ethnic unity law had coincided with the closure of several Tibetan schools, some of which had already been brought under government control.
“These schools could not be shut down before because it was not legally appropriate to do so. Now, with the new Ethnic Unity Law in effect since July, many schools have been closing down,” he told RFA.
“However, many of these schools had already been converted into government-affiliated schools several years ago,” he added.
Dawa Tashi, a researcher at the Tibetan Centre for Human Rights and Democracy in Dharamsala, also linked the closures to the new law, saying it formalized policies that threatened Tibetan cultural and linguistic identity.
A former Tibetan political prisoner who visited Gangjong Grassland Girls’ School in 2006 said many of its graduates had gone on to serve their communities. The source requested anonymity for security reasons.
“I remember speaking with a teacher at the school in 2006 who told me that several teachers had been summoned by Chinese authorities. The teacher anticipated that the school might eventually be closed,” the source told RFA.
New government boarding schools
The closures come amid a broader restructuring of education in Golog, where authorities have promoted Chinese-language education and campaigns emphasizing national unity.
On Sept. 1, 2026 the Golog Education Department officially opened the newly established Golog Tsoshar Middle School in eastern Qinghai. According to Chinese state media, the school enrolled 1,200 students, including 1,090 Tibetans, many from farming and nomadic families.
Authorities have described the relocation of students from Golog to the lower-lying Tsoshar area as part of an effort to expand residential education in the highlands. It remains unclear whether students from Gangjong Grassland Girls’ School were transferred to the new institution.
Golog Ziling (Xining) Middle School, a state-run boarding school in Xining, was also opened on Sept. 1, 2019. According to official figures for 2024, it had 800 students, including 778 Tibetans, all from Golog. The school’s official introduction identifies fostering a shared sense of community among the Chinese nation as a central goal of its education.
In September 2026, the Golog prefecture government also launched a public language promotion week encouraging students to learn and use standard Chinese and emphasizing unity among the Chinese people.
Earlier school closures
The latest shutdowns follow several other closures of Tibetan educational institutions in Golog in recent years.
In July 2024, authorities closed Gangjong Sherig Norling School in Machen County after 30 years of operation. Founded by Jigme Gyaltsen in 1994, the institution had about 1,400 students and 58 teachers and staff.
The vocational school combined modern education with instruction in Tibetan language, culture, philosophy and religion. Reports in April 2025 indicated that authorities had permitted it to reopen as a vocational institution, although its curriculum was expected to change.
Dorjeten National Vocational School in Chikdril County (in Golog) was shut down on Dec. 12, 2025, affecting more than 1,300 students, according to reports. Hungkar Dorje Vocational Secondary School in Golog was also closed on June 24, 2026.
The latest closures have raised further questions about the future of Tibetan-language education in the region and whether students from the affected schools will continue to have opportunities to learn their language and cultural traditions.
Background: The three schools
Gangjong Grassland Girls’ School
Founded in 2005 by Tibetan educator Jigme Gyaltsen in Ragya Township, the school was established to provide education for girls, including those from nomadic communities. When it officially opened on Oct. 15, 2005, it had 203 students and 15 teachers. Its curriculum included Tibetan, Chinese and English, as well as mathematics, science, culture and sports.
Gyaltsen described his educational philosophy as follows: “The education of girls is the education of mothers, and the education of mothers is the foundation of human education.”
Jasag Village Primary School
Established in 1995 with funds raised by local nomadic families through the former Jasag Village Committee, the school served children from the surrounding community. It was renamed Ragya Township Residential School No. 2 in 2008 and closed in September 2026.
Golog Tadra Orphan School
Founded in 2005 by the late Dr. Tawo Lobsang Palden and his wife, Choenyi Lhamo, the school provided education, accommodation, food, clothing and health care to Tibetan orphans and disadvantaged children. Over two decades, it served thousands of children. Lhamo now lives in Germany.

Chief Executive John Lee today congratulated Hong Kong, China athletes on their achievements at the 5th Asian Para Games, commending their outstanding performance and noble sportsmanship.

Mr Lee said the Hong Kong, China delegation delivered an excellent performance at this year's Asian Para Games, winning a total of 41 medals, comprising 3 gold, 14 silver and 24 bronze medals, and achieving Hong Kong's best-ever result in boccia with a total of 2 gold, 3 silver, and 3 bronze medals.

He said these heartening achievements write a splendid chapter in the development of para sports in Hong Kong.

"Hong Kong, China athletes gave their utmost in the competition, demonstrating superb skills and indomitable determination. Their achievements have not only brought honour to Hong Kong, but also inspired the community with their perseverance and never-give-up sportsmanship. Their outstanding performance has earned the admiration and pride of the entire Hong Kong community.”

Mr Lee stressed that the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region Government has always attached great importance to sports development for persons with disabilities, helping them to realise their potential and pursue their dreams. Through the Hong Kong Sports Institute, the Government provides full-time high-level training for elite athletes with disabilities. This allows them to receive professional coaching, with access to barrier-free world-class training venues and equipment, and comprehensive support in sports science and sports medicine, enabling them to represent Hong Kong, China in competitions in the Mainland and abroad.

The Chief Executive added that the Government last year raised the level of direct financial support for elite athletes with disabilities across the board, and for the first time introduced a Senior Squad funding tier. This further enhances the training pathway.

Mr Lee said Hong Kong's outstanding performance at this year's Asian Para Games demonstrates that the Government's policy direction is the right one.

"I would like to thank all the athletes, coaches, medical teams and support personnel for their tireless efforts and dedication. The Government will continue to work closely with the China Hong Kong Paralympic Committee, the Hong Kong Sports Institute and various national sports associations to devote resources to nurturing talent, helping more athletes with disabilities unleash their potential, surpass themselves and achieve new levels in future international competitions."

articles.title: Counter-terrorism exhibition opens
articles.excerpt: The Inter-departmental Counter Terrorism Unit (ICTU) is staging an educational counter-terrorism exhibition in the Hong Kong Museum of History. Co-organised by the National Security Department of the Hong Kong Police Force and co-ordinated by the Security Bureau, the exhibition…
articles.fullText:
The Inter-departmental Counter Terrorism Unit (ICTU) is staging an educational counter-terrorism exhibition in the Hong Kong Museum of History.

Co-organised by the National Security Department of the Hong Kong Police Force and co-ordinated by the Security Bureau, the exhibition aims to enhance public awareness of counter-terrorism (CT) and strengthen public response capabilities through multimedia displays and interactive experiences.

Addressing today's opening ceremony, Secretary for Security Tang Ping-keung emphasised that terrorism knows no borders. He said Hong Kong must therefore remain vigilant and be prepared for potential threats, while continuing to strengthen the city’s CT capabilities in the areas of prevention, preparedness, response and recovery.

Mr Tang outlined that the exhibition aims to deepen public understanding of terrorism, the global CT landscape, and Hong Kong's strategies. It also seeks to encourage members of the public to stay alert, embrace the message that “greater vigilance means lower risk”, and work together to safeguard Hong Kong’s security.

The exhibition, located in the main lobby of the museum, will run until March 1 next year. Together with the National Security Exhibition Gallery on the second floor, it offers a complementary and synergistic exhibition experience.

Featuring diverse and vibrant content across multiple zones, the exhibition showcases the global and local CT landscape; Hong Kong’s strategies, including the Government's Three-tier Prevention Framework for CT, and the relevant legal framework; as well as the CT roles of the ICTU and other government departments.

It also has interactive elements such as the “Spot and Report” and “Run, Hide, Report” games, together with an authentic wartime bomb weighing over 1,000 pounds. Dismantled in 2014, it has been provided for display by the Police Explosive Ordnance Disposal Bureau.

The exhibition enables visitors to gain CT and emergency preparedness knowledge through immersive and interactive experiences, thereby enhancing public awareness of terrorism prevention.

In addition, "Safe Community Plus+”, jointly organised by the ICTU and the Hong Kong Federation of Youth Groups for a third time, also officially launched following the opening ceremony. It will visit various schools and community venues over the next six months, using a variety of interactive mini-games to help students and the public to learn about security awareness and emergency response in an engaging manner.

articles.title: Public alerted to fake messages
articles.excerpt: The Department of Health today alerted the public to suspicious emails and SMS messages sent by its HIV Testing Service website. The department said the email account for the website is suspected of having been misused, with emails and text messages being sent to the public…
articles.fullText:
The Department of Health today alerted the public to suspicious emails and SMS messages sent by its HIV Testing Service website.

The department said the email account for the website is suspected of having been misused, with emails and text messages being sent to the public wrongly indicating that recipients were exposed to Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), and should seek medical advice and get tested as soon as possible.

The department is conducting a thorough investigation into the incident. It said it has not yet found any evidence of data loss or leakage.

Emphasising that the emails and SMS messages were wrongly sent, the department highlighted that it does not notify individuals in this manner. It advised members of the public who receive suspicious emails or SMS messages not to click on any links contained in them or provide personal information. Anyone who has provided personal information to suspicious individuals or suspects that they have been scammed should contact the Police Force.

The department said it immediately conducted a comprehensive inspection of its network system with the outsourced service provider upon discovering the issue last night and also reported it to the force and notified the Digital Policy Office.

The HIV Testing Service website is suspended from today until cybersecurity experts have conducted a comprehensive investigation and review to confirm that there are no security risks. Members of the public can still call the Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome Hotline on 2780 2211 to arrange a free, anonymous and confidential HIV antibody test while the website is suspended.

The Government stressed that it attaches great importance to cybersecurity. The department conducts regular information security risk assessments, and will continue to review and enhance existing measures to keep abreast of the times in order to safeguard network and system security.

The InnoCarnival 2026, showcasing local innovation and technology (I&T) achievements, kicked off today at the Hong Kong Science Park in Sha Tin.

Under the theme "Lead with I&T Dream to Fly High", the event also features an aerospace thematic zone presenting research projects from local universities and their contributions to the country's space exploration missions.

Speaking at the opening ceremony, Financial Secretary Paul Chan said that Hong Kong's strong frontier research capabilities, comprehensive financial services and world-class international talent together provide a complete pathway for turning ideas into industries.

He stressed that Hong Kong's First Five-Year Plan, announced last month, positions the Northern Metropolis as a hub for I&T industries, promoting the integrated development of education, technology, talent and industry to closely align university talent development and research with industry needs. The Government will also leverage Hong Kong's financial strengths to channel more patient capital into supporting research teams and start-ups as they progress from research and development (R&D) to application.

Mr Chan said that I&T development ultimately depends on people, particularly the younger generation, adding that the InnoCarnival encourages public learning through exhibits, workshops, talks and interactive experiences.

Citing a mobile food-waste paper machine that took top prize in the junior secondary division of this year's Hong Kong Student Science Project Competition, Mr Chan urged young people to draw inspiration from everyday life and consider how to make the city a better place.

"The idea is not complicated, but with dedication to putting it into practice, even a small invention can make a big difference. The next invention to reach the world may well come from one of the students here today." he said.

articles.title: Melania Trump secures localised Ukraine truce
articles.excerpt: US first lady Melania Trump has secured a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky, which will begin on October 29, the White House said on Friday. Residents of the southern Ukrainian town, occupied by Russian forces since February 2022…
articles.fullText:
US first lady Melania Trump has secured a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky, which will begin on October 29, the White House said on Friday.

Residents of the southern Ukrainian town, occupied by Russian forces since February 2022, have reported a deepening food crisis.

"Both nations agreed to temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway," a White House statement said.

The development comes as Melania Trump's husband, US President Donald Trump, pressures Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy to reach an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war.

Melania Trump has been active in trying to get Ukrainian children seized by Russia during the war returned to their families.

"The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster. Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water," Melania Trump said in the statement.

The ceasefire will allow non-military teams from both countries to visit residents in their homes and coordinate transportation for those wishing to evacuate to either Russia or Ukraine, with an unnamed American media organisation accompanying the teams to document the process, the first lady said.

Newsmax, a right-leaning news outlet, said in a report that its cameras would be granted "exclusive access to document the effort".

Oleshky, located across the Dnipro River from Kherson, has a remaining population of 1,700 to 2,000 people – primarily elderly residents, along with about 50 children – down from roughly 24,000 before the war, the White House said.

About 90 percent of the city was flooded following the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam, according to the White House.

The statement said Melania Trump and her representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localised ceasefire.

"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” Melania Trump said. (Reuters)

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: Building under construction collapses in Nairobi
articles.excerpt: Many people were feared trapped as a tall building collapsed on Friday in Kenya’s capital, leaving a huge mound of concrete and more than a dozen floors stacked like pancakes, with little space between them. The building was under construction when it collapsed at about 1pm…
articles.fullText:
Many people were feared trapped as a tall building collapsed on Friday in Kenya’s capital, leaving a huge mound of concrete and more than a dozen floors stacked like pancakes, with little space between them.

The building was under construction when it collapsed at about 1pm along a busy commercial street in Nairobi's Eastleigh area, which is often crowded with thousands of traders and residents.

Nairobi police chief Issa Mohamud said the building had more than 10 upper floors under construction.

Rescue operations were complicated, with police firing tear gas at people who had begun looting neighbouring shops, as officers sought to clear the area and provide access to emergency response teams.

Joseph Kaula made it out just in time. A plasterer working on the fifth floor, he said he heard screams and spotted other workers rushing outside, shouting that the building was collapsing.

“I was the last person to walk out before it collapsed and the whole area was filled with dust,” Kaula said.

Kaula suspects a few of his colleagues were trapped in the basement.

One injured woman was rescued and hospitalised, and another person who was crying for help had gone silent, the police chief said.

Mohamud also warned of a possible secondary collapse, as the collapsed building was leaning on its neighbour.

There was little in the way of heavy equipment immediately available. Hours later, a group of rescuers in hard hats were using poles stripped from trees to poke at the huge pile of rubble.

One excavator arrived on site and started moving the concrete bound with steel away so that the rescuers could reach the basement and the ground level, which had been rented out for an electronics shop, a butchery and a grocery while construction continued on the upper floors.

“We are expecting more machines so that we remove those boulders,” the police chief said.

Residents said some of their loved ones who were trapped had made phone calls calling for help immediately after the collapse, but that their phones later became unreachable.

Building collapses are a recurring problem in Nairobi. County officials responsible for issuing building permits have been accused of failing to conduct adequate inspections to ensure developers comply with safety guidelines and construction standards.

“Investigations will be carried out,” Mohamud said. “We’ll make sure people face the law for any negligence.”

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja said the building had been approved for construction, but did not have a certificate of occupation, so opening shops on the ground floor was against the law.

Kenya's county governments need stronger enforcement powers, he said, arguing that lenient penalties for non-compliance are just a “slap on the wrist” for developers that violate regulations. (AP)

articles.title: China’s sanctions on Taiwan allies project its power, but with limited effect
articles.excerpt: Beijing sent a message by sanctioning officials from Paraguay and Belize, but both remain loyal to Taipei.
articles.fullText:
China’s sanctions against foreign officials over their ties with Taiwan help Beijing project power and warn other governments, even as their financial impact and success in curbing engagement remain limited, analysts told Radio Free Asia.
Beijing imposed sanctions on Oct. 12 against Paraguay’s information and communication technologies minister, Gustavo Villate, and Belize’s foreign minister, Francis Fonseca. Both countries maintain formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan rather than China.
China claims Taiwan is an integral part of its territory and considers it a rogue province. Beijing has sought to persuade governments to switch recognition from Taiwan to China, reducing Taiwan’s network of embassies and official government-to-government relationships.
The Chinese government has described the sanctions as a “warning and deterrence.”
The national flags of Paraguay and Taiwan flutter outside the building housing Taiwan's embassy, in Asuncion, Paraguay, Feb. 25, 2026.
(Cesar Olmedo/Reuters) When China sanctions individuals they don’t quite have the same effect as U.S. or European sanctions, Ed Moon, an independent cross-Strait analyst and founder of intelligence site Strait Signal, told RFA.
“Chinese sanctions are unlikely to have significant impacts on people without major interests in the Chinese banking system, shareholdings or business interests,” he said.
But the penalties serve a purpose beyond imposing financial losses, said Moon. They signal to observers in China and abroad that Beijing can enforce restrictions when it believes its interests have been harmed, and can serve as a warning to countries closely connected to the Chinese economy about dealings with sanctioned individuals.
While sanctions could discourage engagement with Taiwan, there is little evidence that the strategy is causing isolation for Taipei, William Yang, a Northeast Asia analyst at the Belgium-based International Crisis Group, told RFA.
“We haven’t really seen a substantial level of retreat in terms of foreign parliamentarians’ trips to Taiwan or foreign governments’ cooperation with Taiwan,” Yang said.
The assessments point to a distinction between two types of sanctions: those that impose measurable costs and those whose principal effect is to publicize Beijing’s opposition to Taiwan’s international relationships.
Isolating Taiwan
Only 12 countries retain formal diplomatic relations with Taipei. Taiwan also maintains extensive unofficial relationships with countries that recognize Beijing. Those ties include trade, investment and parliamentary exchanges, explaining why China’s penalties have targeted politicians beyond Taiwan’s formal diplomatic allies.
Yang said Beijing’s campaign is meant to show Taiwan’s government and people that it has the power to restrict international engagement with Taipei, while simultaneously showing foreign governments that there will be consequences for treating Taiwan as a sovereign state.
He added Beijing believes its economic influence gives it leverage to intimidate politicians and governments considering closer engagement with Taipei.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said during an Oct. 12 press briefing that the ministers from Paraguay and Belize were sanctioned for supporting Taiwan independence through their contacts with Taipei and spreading false allegations about Chinese cyberattacks.
Belize's Prime Minister Johnny Briceno, left, meets with Taiwan's Vice President Lai Ching-te in Honduras, Jan. 27, 2022.
(Taiwan Presidential Office/AP) The next day, Taiwan’s Premier Cho Jung-tai said that Beijing had no right to interfere in Taiwan’s internal affairs or influence its foreign relations. He said Taiwan would continue working with its allies and other democratic governments to defend freedom and democracy and maintain regional peace and security.
Paraguay and Belize also rejected the sanctions. Paraguay’s Foreign Ministry reaffirmed its support for Taiwan, while Belize said the penalties would not alter its foreign policy and defended its relationship with Taipei as a sovereign decision.
Their cooperation involves more than diplomatic recognition. Paraguayan President Santiago Peña visited Taiwan in May, signing agreements covering cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and computing investment, among other areas. Taiwan’s Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung visited Belize in September to deepen bilateral ties.
Do Chinese sanctions work?
Previous cases of Chinese sanctions show the difficulty of turning personal penalties into lasting restrictions on engagement.
In June, China confirmed entry restrictions against New Zealand lawmakers following their visit to Taiwan. Beijing said their trip interfered in China’s internal affairs.
From right to left, Taiwan's Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim, speaking with New Zealand lawmakers Maureen Pugh, Duncan Webb, Laura McClure and David Wilson at the Presidential Office in Taipei, May 7, 2026.
(Presidential Office of Taiwan/AFP) In August 2022, China sanctioned Lithuania’s deputy transport minister, Agnė Vaiciukevičiūtė, after she visited Taiwan. Beijing also suspended exchanges with Vilnius’ transport ministry and paused certain international transportation agreements between the two countries.
That action formed part of a wider dispute after Lithuania allowed a Taiwanese representative office to open in the country in 2021. China downgraded diplomatic relations over the decision.
Cooperation with Taiwan nevertheless continued. Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry reported discussions in April 2026 on strengthening economic and technological ties.
The broader outcome is more complicated. Lithuania’s prime minister described the original representative-office decision as a mistake in February as the country sought to repair relations with Beijing.
Because the dispute involved broader diplomatic and economic pressure, analysts say it is difficult to isolate the impact of sanctions against a single official.
Moon said the same difficulty applied to Paraguay and Belize – Beijing has used various public and private forms of pressure for years, so any subsequent policy change could not automatically be attributed to the latest sanctions.
He said changes in diplomatic language, visits and, at the most dramatic end, diplomatic recognition would provide indicators of whether the relationships were shifting.
Past sanctions have also produced backlash.
In March 2021, Beijing sanctioned European lawmakers and institutions in retaliation for European Union sanctions over human rights abuses in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region. Although the dispute concerned human rights rather than Taiwan, it similarly targeted individual politicians and their institutions.
The European Parliament responded by freezing consideration of an EU-China investment agreement while the Chinese sanctions remained in place. Beijing lifted the sanctions affecting the EU Parliament’s members and committees in 2025.
Moon said sanctions could carry greater economic weight when directed at people or companies with business interests in China, including in Taiwan.
In a separate action on Oct. 14, Beijing announced restrictions against VWAY, a company linked to the father of Taiwanese legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen.
Pedestrians walk past a giant campaign billboard featuring the Democratic Progressive Party's Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen in Taipei on Oct. 15, 2026.
(I-Hwa Cheng/AFP) China’s Taiwan Affairs Office accused Shen’s father of using VWAY to continue trading with Chinese firms after sanctions were placed on another of his businesses.
Moon cautioned that Taiwan-related business sanctions were not directly comparable with penalties against foreign governments’ officials, given Beijing’s position that Taiwan is part of China.
Yang said the sanctions’ limited results so far did not rule out a stronger deterrent effect in the future. Responses by Taiwan’s remaining diplomatic allies, including whether they protested collectively or moved toward recognizing Beijing, would be important to watch, he said.
“So far it seems like at least the government of Paraguay and Belize are holding their lines,” said Yang.
Beijing could still regard the publicity itself as a result, reinforcing its claims over Taiwan and demonstrating that engagement with Taipei carried consequences, Moon said.
“But I think for Beijing the mere fact it has created a news cycle out of the sanctions will mean it has achieved the desired effect of reinforcing its claims over Taiwan and showing there are consequences, however limited, to siding with Taipei.”
Edited by Eugene Whong.

Police on Friday said they arrested two people in Wong Tai Sin, after videos of an 11-year-old girl seeking help went viral on social media.

The Health Bureau on Friday announced the launch of patient pairing arrangements under the Community Pharmacy Programme and the annual adjustment of consultation co-payment fees under the Primary Healthcare Co-care Network.

The bureau said the first phase of the Community Pharmacy Programme, to be trialed in four districts by the end of October, will allow patients to obtain drugs from designated community pharmacies, with pharmacists providing medication counselling and health advice.

The programme is being piloted in Eastern, Yau Tsim Mong, Sha Tin and Yuen Long districts, with five community pharmacies selected in each district.

The bureau said it aims to extend the programme to all 18 districts by the fourth quarter of next year.

Under the programme, participating patients can be paired with a preferred pharmacy for drug dispensing or refill services, a practice that the bureau said would help prevent the accumulation of excess drugs at home and reduce the risk of improper storage or misuse.

Meanwhile, the bureau announced that the annual adjustment of consultation co-payment fees under the Co-care Network will take effect from November 1.

Under the co-payment model, the government provides a partial subsidy while participants pay a set fee.

The bureau said among 1,239 participating service points, 82.5 percent will keep their existing co-payment fees unchanged.

Twenty-eight service points will reduce fees, while 189 will increase them – with nearly 90 percent of those raising fees by HK$50 or below, with the overall rate of increase of 3.7 percent in the coming year, it said.

Following the increase, more than 60 percent of service points will charge consultation co-payments at or below the government-recommended level of HK$150, with the median remaining at HK$150.

As of October 7, more than 300,000 citizens have enrolled in the Co-care Network, with around 70,000 diagnosed with cardiovascular disease risk factors or chronic hepatitis B and having entered the treatment phase.

articles.title: Israel says West Bank operation imminent after attack
articles.excerpt: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday warned of an imminent large-scale military operation in the West Bank and vowed to displace some residents of Hebron after Palestinian gunmen killed two soldiers in an attack. The attack, which happened at a checkpoint near the…
articles.fullText:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday warned of an imminent large-scale military operation in the West Bank and vowed to displace some residents of Hebron after Palestinian gunmen killed two soldiers in an attack.

The attack, which happened at a checkpoint near the Palestinian city in the southern occupied West Bank, also left three soldiers wounded. It came days before Israeli elections in which Netanyahu is facing a tight race.

The two gunmen who carried out the attack were killed in a shootout with soldiers.

In a visit to Hebron after the attack, Netanyahu said Israeli forces would enter the neighbourhood of the attackers and displace its residents.

"We will evacuate the residents, we will go from house to house, we will also seize the weapons there, and all the terrorist infrastructure will be dealt with and destroyed," Netanyahu said, according to his office.

"The defence minister and I are considering a very extensive IDF (army) operation in Judea and Samaria, such as has not been carried out since the Six Day War," Netanyahu added, referring to the 1967 Arab-Israeli war.

"The IDF is ready to execute it and we will set the timing, but it is on the way."

He said the military would apply a model previously used in refugee camps in the northern West Bank.

A large-scale military operation dubbed "Iron Wall" launched in January 2025 forcibly displaced tens of thousands of people across several refugee camps, according to the UN rights office.

As of July this year, 33,362 Palestinian refugees displaced from the three camps had not been permitted to return, according to the UN.

Nearly two years on, Israel's military remains present in Jenin refugee camp, which before Iron Wall was a bastion of armed Palestinian militants fighting Israeli occupation.

The army also remains in two refugee camps in the nearby city of Tulkarem.

In all three camps the army demolished dozens of houses in the dense patchwork of alleys in order to ease access for its troops and armoured vehicles, the military said, and set up operational centres for troops in the homes of residents.

"The Jenin refugee camp model is on its way to Hebron," Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said on X on Friday.

"Every clan neighbourhood in Hebron from which the terrorists emerged today will be evacuated of its residents, and the terror infrastructure in the neighborhood will be addressed and dismantled," he said, referring to the large families, or clans, that hold much influence in the city of Hebron. (AFP)

The nation has allocated 50 million yuan in emergency disaster relief funds and earmarked another 30 million yuan for recovery efforts following a 7.0 magnitude earthquake in southwest Xizang Autonomous Region.

The earthquake struck Baqen County of the city of Nagqu at 10.33pm on Thursday, leaving 16 people dead and 76 injured.

President Xi Jinping has called for all-out rescue efforts.

The Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Emergency Management jointly allocated 50 million yuan to support rescue operations and assistance to affected residents, while the National Development and Reform Commission earmarked the additional 30 million yuan from the central budget to help restore damaged infrastructure and public service facilities.

The country has also upgraded its national earthquake emergency response from Level IV to Level III, while activating a separate Level-IV national natural disaster relief response.

China's national comprehensive fire and rescue force has dispatched a total of 350 rescuers and 83 vehicles.

The emergency management ministry has guided Xizang's emergency management department in arranging for Wing Loong drone deployment to the quake-hit area for disaster reconnaissance.

As of early on Friday, 120 rescuers and 27 vehicles had arrived in the quake-hit area, while the remaining 230 rescuers and 56 vehicles from the Xizang fire and rescue corps were en route as reinforcements, having all entered Nagqu's administrative area.

Earlier, as of 4.30am, authorities had mobilised relief supplies at the central, regional, municipal and county levels, and delivered them in batches to the affected area.

These supplies included 1,000 prefabricated housing units, 3,239 tents, 2,821 folding beds and 4,280 quilts, among other essentials. (Xinhua)

articles.title: iPhone users join the fold as sales begin for Duo
articles.excerpt: Sales of Apple's first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, began on Friday, with market watchers betting on whether the device can reinvent the small foldables market in the same way the iPhone did for smartphones. The Duo's reception could prove an early test for new chief executive…
articles.fullText:
Sales of Apple's first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, began on Friday, with market watchers betting on whether the device can reinvent the small foldables market in the same way the iPhone did for smartphones.

The Duo's reception could prove an early test for new chief executive John Ternus, the former hardware chief who unveiled the phone barely a week after taking charge in September.

It could also have large implications for a niche category in which ⁠rivals such as Samsung Electronics and Huawei Technologies have sold premium offerings for several years.

Within minutes of pre-orders opening last Friday, Apple's estimated delivery dates for the Duo had slipped to late January as demand outpaced supply. The US company called the response from customers "nothing short of extraordinary".

In Sydney, the first Apple store to sell the phones on Friday, a queue of customers formed outside before it opened at 8am.

Simon Krishnan, a 48-year-old engineer, paid A$3,899 for a Duo with 512GB memory.

"This is a bit of a luxury item for me, because it's so expensive, but I just think, you know what? Life's too short," he said.

In China, a soft consumer market combined with memory costs pushing prices higher has led to six straight quarters of declines in smartphone shipments. Apple's market share, however, has rebounded as some phone buyers trade up to premium devices while others seek value at the lower end of the market, putting pressure on mid-range brands.

Liu Wei, a 26-year-old healthcare professional, already has a foldable phone from Xiaomi, but still queued outside a central Shanghai Apple store from 6am to get his hands on Apple's first foldable.

"I've used Apple products for many years and I have more trust [in the brand], so I bought one on launch day to try it out," he said.

In Hong Kong, May, 38, secured a 256GB iPhone Duo, which retails for HK$17,499, during an online pre-sale and aimed to resell the handset for a profit of around HK$4,000: “A few meals' worth of money,” he joked.

The limited supplies could disappoint Apple fans lining up in front of stores to buy the Duo. Apple has said walk-in availability would vary by jurisdictions and, with limited stocks in the US, Australia, Canada, Mexico and much of Britain and Europe. In Hong Kong, the Chinese mainland, France, India and Japan, units would be available only for customers who had ordered online. (Reuters)

Hong Kong, China on Friday continued to shine in table tennis at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya, bagging a silver and a bronze in the men's and women's doubles events.

With no third-place play-off, Hong Kong were guaranteed of at least bronze entering the day's last four matches at Sky Hall Toyota.

The SAR pair of Chiu Kan-shan and Wong Yue-ching claimed silver in women's doubles class WD14 event, after falling to the national team's Huang Wenjuan and Liu Xiaowu in straight games.

Huang and Liu needed just 23 minutes to wrap up the one-sided affair, sweeping to a 5-11, 8-11, 8-11 victory.

Fellow paddlers Ho Ka-sing and Wong Chi-yin added to Hong Kong's medal tally by winning bronze in the semis of the men's doubles class MD18 event.

They fell 1-3 to China's Lian Hao and Zhao Shuai.

Ho and Wong put up a spirited fight despite dropping the first game 8-11, taking the second 11-7 to level the best-of-five contest.

But the SAR pair were unable to maintain their momentum, losing the next two games 2-11, 7-11 to claim bronze after 24 minutes.

articles.title: Apec finance chiefs' meet 'perfect prelude to summit'
articles.excerpt: Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui said on Friday the Apec Finance Ministers' Meeting that concluded in Hong Kong on Wednesday was the "perfect prelude" to the leaders' summit in Shenzhen next month. He told RTHK's Backchat programme that Hong Kong…
articles.fullText:
Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui said on Friday the Apec Finance Ministers' Meeting that concluded in Hong Kong on Wednesday was the "perfect prelude" to the leaders' summit in Shenzhen next month.

He told RTHK's Backchat programme that Hong Kong and Shenzhen have plenty of room to work together – making it a great opportunity to showcase both China's stabilising role and Hong Kong's part in driving regional cooperation.

"Even though this is really a China Apec year this year, but at the same time, Hong Kong plays a critical role as an accelerator of regionalisation," Hui said.

He pointed out the finance ministers' meeting was the last in a series of ministerial meetings before the leaders' summit and that a joint statement had been reached among delegates – a breakthrough in an increasingly divided geopolitical landscape.

"So, it's indeed a very good occasion for us to showcase not just the China voice as a stabiliser but also Hong Kong's element as an accelerator of regionalisation in this increasingly divided world," Hui said.

"Hong Kong, being part of Asia and at the same time a financial centre of Asia, needs to have a stable Asia."

Delegates, Hui said, agreed to work more closely on fiscal and monetary policy coordination, digital infrastructure, green finance and talent cultivation.

He also highlighted the need for inclusive policies to address income and wealth distribution risks arising from artificial intelligence and geopolitics.

There is a "wide consensus" that AI is a double-edged sword, Hui pointed out, in its presenting opportunities alongside risks including cyber threats.

He said Hong Kong has practical experiences to share, as many financial institutions in the city are already adopting AI across their value chains.

"Hong Kong has a lot to share and offer in terms of how we do that and also find a fine line between regulation and also AI application," Hui said, adding the city has developed its own ecosystem for AI deployment in financial infrastructure.

On gold trading, he said the subject came up in his bilateral meeting with Brunei's finance minister.

Hong Kong, Hui stressed, aims to serve as an Asia hub linking international gold standards with regional liquidity.

"Gold, as it is, is a global product, yet at the same time there is ever-stronger demand for such precious metals here in the region," he said.

Reflecting on the organisation of the event, Hui credited his colleagues across government for their hard work, saying the effort had paid off.

"I heard that some of the delegates are going to get married here in Hong Kong because they see Hong Kong as a very decent place, and they're going to spend their honeymoon here," he said, adding that the city's "charisma" had helped deliver a pleasing result for the country and the world.

articles.title: Chinalco sets up treasury centre in Hong Kong
articles.excerpt: Aluminum Corporation of China, known as Chinalco, has established a corporate treasury centre in Hong Kong to manage the state-owned giant's offshore funds, Invest Hong Kong announced on Friday. The new entity, Chinalco Treasury Management Co Ltd, will centrally manage the…
articles.fullText:
Aluminum Corporation of China, known as Chinalco, has established a corporate treasury centre in Hong Kong to manage the state-owned giant's offshore funds, Invest Hong Kong announced on Friday.

The new entity, Chinalco Treasury Management Co Ltd, will centrally manage the group's offshore funds and handle offshore financing, exchange rate and interest rate risk management, as well as integrated financial services.

Director-General of Investment Promotion Alpha Lau said the move demonstrates Hong Kong's strengths as the first port of call for mainland firms going global and as a hub for corporate treasury centres.

"As the world's largest offshore renminbi hub, Hong Kong can provide enterprises with cross-border renminbi settlement, multi-currency fund management and risk hedging capabilities," Lau said.

She added that she hopes Chinalco will use the treasury centre as a starting point to further establish commodity trading functions in Hong Kong, combining the city's pricing, clearing, financing, and warehousing networks with the company's own industrial strengths to create synergy.

Chinalco Chief Financial Officer Wang Xin said Hong Kong's foreign exchange market – the fourth largest in the world – together with its well-developed channels for renminbi financing and trade settlement, and its unique advantage of connecting to the mainland, will help the group manage its global funds in a more efficient and effective way.

"In the future, Chinalco Treasury will build a fully functional offshore fund management platform for the group. All funds will be pooled, all settlement will be centralised and all risks will be controlled," she said.

Founded in 2001, Chinalco is a key state-owned enterprise under the direct administration of the central government, with an industrial chain covering more than 20 non-ferrous metals. It has been on the Fortune Global 500 list every year since 2008 and operates in more than 20 countries and regions.
