articles.fullText:
The Immigration Department said manpower was deployed to handle an expected increase in inbound passengers at Huanggang port on Monday, at the end of the long Chung Yeung Festival weekend travel rush.

Officials said operations at the redeveloped port were generally smooth thus far.

The Security Bureau said about 9,400 people arrived in Hong Kong via Huanggang port between 2pm and 4pm.

Travellers were urged to be patient and follow the instructions of immigration staff and police.

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: Li calls for stronger China-Tajikistan cooperation
articles.excerpt: Premier Li Qiang said on Monday that China is willing to expand cooperation with Tajikistan in emerging industries such as the digital economy and artificial intelligence. In his meeting with Tajik President Emomali Rahmon in Dushanbe, Li said China stands ready to expand…
articles.fullText:
Premier Li Qiang said on Monday that China is willing to expand cooperation with Tajikistan in emerging industries such as the digital economy and artificial intelligence.

In his meeting with Tajik President Emomali Rahmon in Dushanbe, Li said China stands ready to expand bilateral trade with Tajikistan, strengthen cooperation in infrastructure, green minerals, connectivity and other fields, so as to jointly build new drivers of economic growth.

He also called for deepening cooperation in law enforcement and security.

Li arrived in Tajikistan on Sunday for an official visit and to attend the 25th meeting of the Council of Heads of Government (Prime Ministers) of Member States of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO).

In talks with Iran's First Vice President Mohammad-Reza Aref on the sidelines of the SCO meeting, the premier said Beijing stands ready to promote new progress in exchanges and cooperation across various fields with Tehran.

Li also said China, upholding the spirit of the series of major initiatives and proposals put forward by President Xi Jinping, will continue to work to promote peace, stability and development in the Middle East.

He added that sovereignty and security of all countries should be respected, and that all parties concerned should opt for peace, resume dialogue and negotiations at an early date, and resolve differences through political and diplomatic means. (Reporting by Xinhua)

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: Operators urged to monitor Huanggang transport flows
articles.excerpt: Commissioner for Transport Winnie Tse urged the sector on Monday to monitor passenger and vehicle flows in real time at Huanggang port and to remain alert and deploy resources in a flexible manner to meet the needs of travellers. The call came as the crossing was set to face…
articles.fullText:
Commissioner for Transport Winnie Tse urged the sector on Monday to monitor passenger and vehicle flows in real time at Huanggang port and to remain alert and deploy resources in a flexible manner to meet the needs of travellers.

The call came as the crossing was set to face peak crowds with people returning home following the long Chung Yeung Festival weekend.

In a social media post, the Transport Department said it was undertaking multiple measures with operators to keep traffic around the crossing running smoothly.

It said about 120 franchised buses, 40 scheduled‑route minibuses and 130 cross‑boundary coaches would be deployed to provide services as well as be on standby in case of heavy passengers flows.

During busy periods, franchised bus frequencies can be increased to every two to three minutes while scheduled minibuses and cross‑boundary coaches may run every three to four minutes and franchised operators will also run extra short‑haul trips to ease overcrowding.

The department also noted that operators had installed clear signages and facilities to help people queue in an orderly manner as well as deployed service ambassadors and operational staff at key locations to assist travellers.

The Immigration Department recorded more than 1.32 million crossings – more than 690,000 departures and nearly 630,000 arrivals – through all checkpoints on Sunday, with departures by Hong Kong residents exceeding 530,000.

Of the inbound arrivals, mainland visitors numbered over 98,000.

Huanggang port recorded about 152,000 arrivals and departures – the highest since the crossing opened — with Hong Kong residents accounting for more than 66,000.

The busiest crossing remained Lo Wu with nearly 260,000, followed by Lok Ma Chau Spur Line with more than 200,000.

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: China's GDP rebounds to beat expectations
articles.excerpt: China's economic growth rebounded to 4.5 percent year on year in the third quarter, beating expectations and easing the pressure on policymakers for delivering more aggressive stimulus measures to meet the annual target. The gross domestic product growth rate, released by the…
articles.fullText:
China's economic growth rebounded to 4.5 percent year on year in the third quarter, beating expectations and easing the pressure on policymakers for delivering more aggressive stimulus measures to meet the annual target.

The gross domestic product growth rate, released by the National Bureau of Statistics on Monday, beat the forecast for 4.4 percent growth in a poll and was an improvement from the more-than-three-year low of 4.3 percent in the April-to-June period.

The world's second-largest economy generated about 107.11 trillion yuan in output in the first three quarters.

Beijing has leaned heavily on exports for growth this year, but that engine faces growing pressure as domestic demand remains weak and trade tensions with the European Union escalate.

China's strategy of redirecting credit and resources from property towards high-tech industries has created a two-speed economy, where strong factory output and exports mask weak consumption and private investment.

For January-September, the economy grew 4.6 percent, within the range of the government's annual growth target of 4.5 to five percent.

On a quarterly basis, the economy expanded 1.2 percent in the third quarter, surpassing expectations for a 1.1 percent rise and accelerating from 0.9 percent in April-June.

The trade surplus widened more than expected in September as exports surged, keeping the country on track to surpass last year's record surplus of US$1.2 trillion and likely intensifying trade tensions with major partners.

A deal with the EU to rein in Chinese hybrid-vehicle shipments could weigh on the booming auto trade.

Beijing has recently expanded support for home buyers, unveiled measures to steer cheaper credit into sectors such as infrastructure and technology and allocated 550 billion yuan in unused government debt quotas to ease local governments' financial strain and expand infrastructure investment.

Authorities also stepped up fiscal support, including expanding loan interest subsidies for small private firms and consumers and tapping an 800 billion yuan policy-based financing tool to spur infrastructure investment.

Still, infrastructure investment shrank 4.2 percent.

Fixed-asset investment declined 7.2 percent in the first nine months, dropping at the same pace as in January-to-August period.

Retail sales grew 1.1 percent in September, though, improving from the 0.4 percent rise in August and compared with an expected 0.6 percent rise.

It marked the quickest growth since March.

For the first three quarters, total retail sales of goods and services, a major indicator of the country's consumption strength, increased by 2.6 percent.

Property investment fell 20.6 percent during the period.

Policymakers refrained from releasing large-scale stimulus measures, as strong goods exports, aided by a global AI-fuelled tech boom, should help the country reach its annual growth target.

Industrial output expanded 5.5 percent in September, accelerating from the 5.2 percent growth in August and was in line with expectations.

It marked the quickest growth in six months.

For the first three quarters, value-added industrial output increased by 5.3 percent. (Xinhua/Reuters)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Davidovich Fokina reigns supreme in Shanghai
articles.excerpt: Alejandro Davidovich Fokina ended Rafael Jodar's dream run at the Shanghai Masters on Sunday, battling back to beat his fellow Spaniard 1-6 7-6(5) 6-4 and clinch the biggest title of his career. The 25th-seeded Davidovich Fokina is set to climb 13 places to a career-high world…
articles.fullText:
Alejandro Davidovich Fokina ended Rafael Jodar's dream run at the Shanghai Masters on Sunday, battling back to beat his fellow Spaniard 1-6 7-6(5) 6-4 and clinch the biggest title of his career.

The 25th-seeded Davidovich Fokina is set to climb 13 places to a career-high world number 13 when the rankings are released on Monday.

Jodar, playing in his first Masters 1000 final and the youngest Shanghai finalist in tournament history, made a blistering start, broke for a 2-0 lead and again to take the opening set.

Davidovich Fokina recovered from a break down in the second set and saved break points in three successive service games before edging a tight tiebreak to force a decider.

The momentum swung decisively in Davidovich Fokina's favour when he broke the 12th-seeded Jodar twice and sealed victory in two hours and 27 minutes.

"I have a blank mind," Davidovich Fokina said. "I don't know what to say and I don't know how I feel. Just a huge relief.

"After the first set I had to keep trying, keep pushing. In the tiebreak, I believed in myself again. In the third set, maybe I had a bit more fitness physically."

It's the third ATP singles title of the 27-year-old's career, adding to his ATP 250 triumphs in Chengdu and Mallorca this season.

The first meeting between the two Spaniards pitted one of the ATP Tour's rising talents against a player enjoying the best season of his career.

The 20-year-old Jodar, who was ranked outside the world's top 900 little more than a year ago, strengthened his bid to qualify for the ATP Finals in Turin in his first full season on tour. (Reuters)

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: Uyghur activists urge Rubio to raise rights concerns with Central Asian officials
articles.excerpt: Uzbekistan trip is a chance to reassert U.S. moral leadership by pressing the C5 to protect Uyghur communities.
articles.fullText:
Uyghur advocates have urged U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to seek commitments not to deport Uyghurs to China and to protect them from Beijing’s transnational repression during his upcoming meetings with Central Asian officials, the leader of a prominent Uyghur rights organization told Radio Free Asia.
Rubio is leading a U.S. delegation of more than 200 business representatives and will arrive in Uzbekistan on Saturday for the first leg of a six-day trip that also includes two stops in India. While in Samarkand, he will attend the C5+1 ministerial meetings – with officials from the five Central Asian countries of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio boards a plane, Oct. 8, 2026, in Lisbon.
(Mark Schiefelbein/AP) According to the Washington-based Uyghur Human Rights Project, more than 400,000 Uyghurs live in these Central Asian countries and combined they form the “vast majority” of the Uyghur diaspora outside of East Turkestan, which is the name by which Uyghurs call their homeland, currently under the control of the People’s Republic of China.
As a U.S. senator, Rubio was a champion of Uyghur issues and now as Washington’s top diplomat, he is expected to discuss the safety and rights of Uyghurs with the C5 leaders, Abdureshit Abdulhamit, vice president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress, told RFA.
Abdureshit Abdulhamit, vice president of the World Uyghur Congress.
(RFA Illustration) “We urge him to seek clear commitments that no Uyghur will be forcibly returned to China, where they could face persecution, imprisonment or torture,” said Abdureshit. “Uyghurs seeking protection should have access to fair asylum procedures.”
He also urged Rubio to address intimidation and surveillance targeting Uyghur communities, saying people should be able to preserve their culture, discuss detained relatives and communicate abroad without fear.
Communities at risk
Compared to Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, Uyghurs in Uzbekistan face more challenges to their social and cultural rights, Zumretay Erkin, another vice president of the organization, told RFA.
“Uzbekistan is also complicit in deporting Uyghurs to China at the explicit request of the Chinese government,” she said. “Uyghurs are subjected to tight surveillance and transnational repression.”
Zumretay Erkin, vice president of the World Uyghur Congress.
(RFA Illustration) Zumretay said Rubio’s diplomatic visit is a “unique opportunity to raise Uyghur human rights, even in a trade and investment context,” noting that the U.S. government was among the first to take action to address the Uyghur genocide.
Washington classified China’s treatment of Uyghurs in the Uyghur region as genocide in 2021.
Moral leadership
Rubio can show the world that the United States’ moral leadership still matters, Omer Kanat, executive director of the Washington-based Uyghur Human Rights Project, wrote in an opinion piece in The Diplomat.
Kanat cited former U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo’s public calls against returning Uyghurs to China as a precedent. He also pointed to Thailand’s February 2025 deportation of 40 Uyghurs as a warning of the consequences when diplomatic efforts fail.
Omer Kanat, executive director of the Uyghur Human Rights Project.
(RFA Illustration) “This upcoming trip to Central Asia gives Rubio a chance to show that the United States won’t countenance a repeat of that tragedy,” he wrote. “With the right messaging, the trip can fortify China’s neighbors to stand firm against Beijing’s pressure to return Uyghurs to China.”
The WUC also called on Rubio to hear directly from Uyghur representatives and establish follow-up mechanisms for individual cases.
“We would judge the visit by concrete results: stronger protection against deportation, action on cases of harassment and a clear American commitment to follow through after the meetings end,” said Abdureshit.
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Tibetan rights group: South Africa arson attack is transnational repression by CCP
articles.excerpt: Police are still investigating the firebombing of the Dalai Lama representative’s home office in South Africa.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Tibetan.
Authorities are still investigating Wednesday’s firebombing of the Dalai Lama’s representative office in South Africa, police told Radio Free Asia, as activists accused China of having a hand in the attack.
'Transnational repression' by China, Tibet activists say
The office of the Tibetan spiritual leader in Pretoria suffered extensive damage in the 11 p.m. attack, but nobody was hurt, the representative Dhondup Gyalpo told RFA.
“I heard the sound of breaking glass and saw smoke coming into the house. As soon as I realized what was happening, I broke a window and got outside,” he said. “Another firebomb that had not exploded was hanging above the window. I was slightly injured by broken glass.”
A fire burns at the residence and office of Dhondup Gyalpo, the Dalai Lama’s representative in South Africa, in Lyttelton Manor, Centurion, outside Pretoria, Oct. 14, 2026.
(Dhondup Gyalpo) Shortly after the fire brigade extinguished the blaze, the crime scene experts and detectives arrived to investigate, but no suspects have been arrested,” police spokesperson Brigadier BM Muridili, told RFA.
Wednesday’s firebombing was the second such attack on the office in months. The office had previously been firebombed in July, on the Dalai Lama’s 91st birthday. Gyalpo described Wednesday’s attack in detail.
“The Molotov cocktail used in the attack produced more smoke than flames. At first, it looked as though the entire building was on fire,” he said. “When I entered, the smoke was so thick and overpowering that I could almost taste it.”
The fire engulfed parts of the property, causing extensive damage to the building, furniture and official documents, he said. Neither Gyalpo nor Khenpo Jamyang Gonpo, a staff member at the office, was injured in the fire.
“Transnational repression”
The attacks on the Dalai Lama’s office are part of a “global rise in transnational repression” by the Chinese Communist Party against the Tibetan people, the New York-based rights group Students for a Free Tibet said in a statement.
“Students for a Free Tibet urges South African law enforcement and government authorities to conduct an immediate, thorough, and independent investigation,” the group said. “Law enforcement must not dismiss these attacks as ordinary local crime, but must explicitly examine political motives and potential foreign state involvement.”
The Desmond & Leah Tutu Legacy Foundation also condemned Wednesday’s attack in a statement and called for stronger protections of freedom of expression, religion and association.
Desmond Tutu and the Dalai Lama are both Nobel laureates for their nonviolent struggles, and in the statement, the foundation noted their long friendship.
The Dalai Lama speaks with Archbishop Desmond Tutu in Seattle, April 15, 2008.
(Ted S. Warren/AP) “We stand with the Tibetan community in South Africa and with everyone who lives and works at the Office,” the foundation said. “No community in South Africa should have to go to sleep wondering whether their home will be set alight because of who they are, where they come from or what they believe.”
Gyalpo said he suspected that the attack might be politically motivated, but cautioned that the perpetrators and their motives have not been identified yet.
“There seems to be a warning sign intended to intimidate us but we are not scared,” he said. “We have no reason to hate the people of South Africa and there is also no reason why the people of South Africa should not like us,” he said.
Edited by Tawang in Tibetan and Eugene Whong and Charlie Dharapak in English.

articles.title: China covered up the cause of a detained Uyghur father’s death
articles.excerpt: Police confirm to RFA that Yasinjan Toxti died in their custody in 2018, not in a traffic accident.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Uyghur
Chinese authorities in 2018 lied to the family of a Uyghur bus driver who died in their custody, an investigation by Radio Free Asia has revealed.
Authorities told the family of Yasinjan Toxti, who had been detained in a “re-education” facility on suspicion of “religious radicalism,” that he had died in a car accident.
Yasinjan’s sister Reyhangul told RFA that the details did not add up. A resident of Belgium, Reyhangul discussed the moment in 2018 when her younger sister in the Uyghur region told her of her brother’s death.
“How could someone held in ‘re-education’ die in a traffic accident?” she recalled asking. She said her sister replied, “That is what the police told us. We have to accept that explanation. Under the current circumstances, we cannot ask any further questions about it.”
2018 was the height of China’s Uyghur internment campaign aimed at “curbing terrorism” where an estimated 1.8 million Uyghurs were put in detainment facilities claimed by authorities to be vocational training centers. The U.S. in 2020 classified Beijing’s actions in the Uyghur region as a genocide.
Inconsistencies uncovered
In an attempt to gain more clarity on the circumstances of Yasinjan’s death, RFA this month telephoned the Qartal Bazaar police station in Aksu, an oasis city in the Uyghur region, where Yasinjan lived and worked.
Two separate police personnel shared information that conflicted with what authorities told Reyhangul’s family in 2018.
The chief of the police station was the first to answer RFA’s questions.
RFA spoke to the chief of police in Aksu, Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.
(RFA Illustration) A police officer on duty provided further details.
RFA spoke to a police officer in Aksu, Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.
(RFA Illustration) In assessing that Yasinjan had been in detention for “five or six months,” the police chief may have been referring to his cumulative time in re-education across multiple sentences, and the police officer who said he was taken to the hospital after “nine or 10 days” may have been referring to the length of time into his latest sentence. RFA was unable to confirm what either expression of time meant exactly.
Educational pursuits
Yasinjan was born in 1980 in Aksu and lived there his entire life. Having received only a primary school education himself, Yasinjan saw the importance of education and sent his five-year-old son, Hebibulla Yasin, to study in Egypt. His sister was already living in Egypt overseeing her own children’s education, and agreed to be Hebibulla’s caretaker there.
Sending children abroad for educational purposes was at the time common for many Uyghur families, because China had been expanding its policy of “bilingual education,” – which in practice was replacing the Uyghur language with Mandarin Chinese for most classes.
Many Uyghur parents viewed this as accelerating assimilation, and feared their children would lose their Uyghur cultural and religious identity. Egypt, which had a strong reputation for Islamic education, and relatively low living costs, was a natural choice for families wishing to preserve their culture.
Before 2017, more than 5,000 Uyghurs were living in Egypt, but mass arrests by the Chinese government under the “Strike Hard Campaign Against Violent Terrorism” intensified the next year . Arrests often targeted Uyghurs with family members abroad, especially in “sensitive” Muslim majority countries like Turkey and Egypt.
Arousing suspicion
Because his son was in Egypt, Yasinjan was detained several times between 2016 and 2018 on suspicion of “religious radicalism” and subjected to short periods of “re-education,” according to Reyhangul. Authorities were able to compel Yasinjan to bring Hebibulla home, but even after his son returned, Yasinjan remained under suspicion.
Yasinjan was in custody four separate times between 2016 and 2018. His latest detention was for stopping the bus in the middle of his route to allow Muslim passengers to observe the call to prayer.
It was during this latest detention that he died – not of a traffic accident as Reyhangul said authorities previously claimed – but after arriving in a “re-education camp” as confirmed by police in RFA’s investigation.
Years after Yasinjan’s death, while Reyhangul was searching for more information, she learned that other members of her family had been detained – her sister, who had told her about their brother’s death, for “leaking state secrets,” and her mother, who had traveled to Turkey, for “visiting a sensitive country.”
Still, Reyhangul does not know where they are detained, nor the length of their sentences, she said.
Edited by Eugene Whong and Charlie Dharapak.

articles.title: MPF schemes notice published
articles.excerpt: The Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes (General) (Amendment) Regulation 2025 will come into operation on December 21, following a notice published today in the Government Gazette. This commencement notice facilitates the rollout of Phase One of Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) "Full…
articles.fullText:
The Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes (General) (Amendment) Regulation 2025 will come into operation on December 21, following a notice published today in the Government Gazette.

This commencement notice facilitates the rollout of Phase One of Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) "Full Portability". Under the Amendment Regulation, employees whose employment began on or after May 1 last year (New EEs) will be permitted to transfer the entirety of their accrued benefits derived from employer mandatory contributions in respect of their current employment.

These funds can be moved from the employer’s chosen MPF scheme to a personal account of an MPF scheme of their own choice. Transfers can be made once every calendar year, or more frequently if permitted by the governing rules of the transferring MPF scheme.

Secretary for Financial Services & the Treasury Christopher Hui stated that with the implementation of Phase One "Full Portability" on December 21, the Government has fulfilled its commitment outlined in the 2026 Policy Address. He noted that this change will give new employees greater control over their MPF benefits, encourage more proactive management of their investments, stimulate market competition, and create room for fee reductions.

Mr Hui added that the Government is currently drafting legislative proposals for Phase Two "Full Portability", which will extend these benefits to the remaining workforce. The corresponding amendment bill is scheduled to be introduced to the Legislative Council by mid-2027.

The commencement notice will be tabled before the Legislative Council next Wednesday for negative vetting.

articles.title: China’s TNR: Three communities, three phases, one evolving system
articles.excerpt: RFA convened a closed, bipartisan roundtable on Capitol Hill, “China’s Transnational Repression (TNR)
articles.fullText:
WASHINGTON—Ahead of Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington, D.C. in September, Radio Free Asia (RFA) convened a closed, bipartisan roundtable on Capitol Hill, “China’s Transnational Repression (TNR): Three Communities, Three Phases, One Evolving System”—examining trends and developments regarding the targeting of Tibetan, Uyghur, and Hong Kong diaspora communities and groups. RFA, uniquely positioned to host the roundtable, has both documented TNR’s rise and has been a target.
From that discussion with Congressional staff, policymakers, rights advocates, academics, and journalists, RFA is reporting out a set of recommendations and ideas regarding TNR’s development, growth, and sophistication. Issues raised were ways of protecting journalists and advocates, TNR’s use by Beijing as a tactic aimed at manipulating global narratives, artificial intelligence’s role in expanding its scope, its growing presence on U.S. soil , including universities and diaspora communities, and Beijing’s growing influence with international institutions, such as Interpol, to aid its efforts.
“From RFA’s exclusive reporting on restrictions of religious freedom in Tibet and forced labor and human rights abuses in Xinjiang, to closing our physical bureau in Hong Kong after authorities enacted Article 23 and named us a ‘foreign force,’ RFA and our journalists have endured every iteration of TNR designed to silence us and inhibit transparency,” RFA President and CEO Bay Fang said.
Delivering opening remarks at the roundtable was Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-OR), former Chair of the Congressional-Executive Commission on China (CECC), who introduced the bipartisan Transnational Repression Policy Act (S.2525) last year, co-sponsored by current CECC Chair Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK). The conversation, moderated by RFA’s Chief Communications Officer Rohit Mahajan, delved into the issues outlined above, with an eye on fostering greater cross-sector cooperation, understanding, and solutions.
RFA plans to continue engaging on this issue with partners, policymakers, authorities, technologists, freedom advocates, journalists, and experts in this critical space.
Read the chief takeaways from RFA’s session here: https://docs.rfa.org/english/docs/RFA_TNR_Roundtable_Sept.2026.pdf .

articles.title: After US accuses Fijian of corruption for China, experts warn of region-wide network
articles.excerpt: “Illicit disruptors” in Pacific allow Beijing to benefit from illegal activity while offering plausible deniability
articles.fullText:
Beijing’s corruption and influence operations are not limited to Fiji, and similar operations likely exist in other Pacific island countries, experts on the region told Radio Free Asia.
The analysis came shortly after Washington accused Fijian national Zhao Fugang of corruption as head of the Overseas Chinese Service Center in Suva.
“Zhao abused his public position by paying bribes to Fijian citizens to advance China-based government, business, and criminal interests,” U.S. State Department spokesman Thomas Pigott said in a statement. “His actions constituted significant corruption and adversely affected U.S. interests in Fiji.”
Though Zhao is now barred from entering the United States, there are probably more people involved in the type of corruption he is accused of – not just in Fiji, but across the entire Pacific region, Gregory Brown, executive director of the Washington-based Alliance Futures Initiative think tank, told RFA.
“I seriously doubt that Beijing set up a corruption and influence operation in Fiji and then decided not to replicate it anywhere else in a region where it’s spending billions on infrastructure, signing security agreements, and competing every day for political influence,” said Brown. “That defies logic and everything we know about the CCP’s overseas influence campaigns. There is no reason similar operations wouldn’t work in Honiara, Port Moresby, Nuku’alofa, or Port Vila.”
A map showing the location of Fiji within the Pacific region.
(AFP) Illicit activities that advance Chinese interests occur elsewhere in the Pacific, Kathryn Paik, deputy director of the Australia Chair at the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies, told RFA.
“There have been many documented cases of Chinese actors in other Pacific countries and territories conducting illegal activities such as drug trafficking, illegal fishing, money laundering, and more,” said Paik. “What is key is that while most if not all of these actors may not be an official Chinese agent, they are conducting activity that is either encouraged by or facilitated by Beijing.”
Illicit disruptors
Zhao is an example of China’s use of “state-condoned illicit disruptors as a form of gray zone activity in the Pacific,” José Sousa-Santos, of the University of Canterbury in New Zealand, wrote in an essay published in Small Wars Journal , a project by the Future Security Initiative at Arizona State University.
Written months before the U.S. sanctioned Zhao – who Australian law enforcement had already identified as having connections to organized crime – the essay detailed how Beijing tolerates and protects criminal figures and networks to serve objectives of the state.
“This does not require a simple command relationship between the Chinese state and organized crime. Nor does it mean that every Chinese criminal actor abroad is an agent of Beijing,” wrote Sousa-Santos. “The more important point is that certain illicit actors can become strategically useful when they extend influence, cultivate local elites, generate deniable economic leverage, support patriotic narratives, and operate in spaces where formal state power would attract resistance.”
Actors like Zhao are valuable in that Beijing can deny all connections of involvement in their illegal activities, all while benefiting from them, the essay said.
“Zhao’s value is that he represents the kind of high-risk intermediary who can move money, cultivate elites, open doors, normalize Chinese influence, and generate dependency while remaining formally outside the state,” it said.
After the U.S. sanctioned Zhao, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told a news conference she had no knowledge of his case.
“We oppose vilification and smears against China,” she said.
Cooperation needed
In a Facebook post, the Fijian government asked Washington to provide evidence of the allegations against Zhao, and affirmed Suva’s commitment to work with international partners to crack down on transnational crime.
The U.S. and its allies should coordinate with each other to stop illicit activities, Paik said.
“Working collaboratively to identify illegal activity and name specific actors is certainly a start,” she said. “But of course Pacific countries are sovereign nations and the next step will ideally be to take action against these individuals in whichever country they are acting.”
Brown said that the U.S. should not stop with its sanctions on Zhao, but should name other individuals in the region to demonstrate how widespread the problem is.
“If we see three or four more across different Pacific countries in the next six months, the signal becomes a pattern,” he said.
Brown also called for the U.S. and its allies to support Pacific governments in building their own anti-corruption and counter-intelligence capacity, urged Pacific governments to make foreign-linked community organizations more accountable by requiring them to register, and work together to protect Chinese diaspora communities in the region.
“My big question now is whether this designation is a one-off or a campaign,” he said. “If it’s a one-off, Beijing will absorb the hit and move on. If it’s a campaign, it’s a chance to change calculus for every Chinese operative and every compromised Pacific official in the region.”
Edited by Charlie Dharapak.

articles.title: Kindergarten profiles released online
articles.excerpt: The Education Bureau today released the latest online profiles of local kindergartens and childcare centres to help parents make informed school choices for their children. The dedicated website provides information on about 930 kindergartens and childcare centres in Hong Kong…
articles.fullText:
The Education Bureau today released the latest online profiles of local kindergartens and childcare centres to help parents make informed school choices for their children.

The dedicated website provides information on about 930 kindergartens and childcare centres in Hong Kong, including the approved fees for all kindergartens for the 2026-27 academic year. It also identifies kindergartens participating in the kindergarten education scheme.

The profiles display each institution's approved fees after government subsidies are deducted, alongside their official quality review results. Furthermore, parents can access details regarding the professional qualifications of staff and total numbers of teachers.

The website also features enrolment figures, teacher-to-pupil ratios, curriculum information, and reference prices for major education items, application and registration fees.

Additionally, the profiles include dedicated columns outlining the specific support available for non-Chinese speaking students, as well as the resources offered for children with special needs.

articles.title: Exclusive: North Korean army video says K-drama watchers deserve to be executed
articles.excerpt: Used in ideological training sessions, the video calls offenders as “traitors” who “gouged out their own eyes.”
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Korean
A North Korean video warns soldiers that they could be punished - and they should be executed - for watching foreign media, a recording obtained exclusively by Radio Free Asia reveals.
North Korean army video says K-drama watchers deserve to be executed
A female narrator with a booming voice denounces soldiers for not resisting the temptation to watch “impure recordings” like South Korean TV shows and Hollywood films.
The footage obtained by RFA is a recording of a screen showing the video. It is believed to have been produced in 2023 and is still in use in soldiers’ ideological training sessions, sources inside the country told RFA on condition of anonymity for security reasons.
“I strongly demand, on behalf of all military personnel, the summary execution of those who have become thoroughly steeped in the rotten imperialist ideology, culture and way of life,” the narrator says. She calls for the “relentless pursuit and capture” of those who watch foreign media so that they can be “subjected to merciless punishment.”
The educational video presents the cautionary tales of at least two military personnel who were caught watching foreign media, detailing how they were punished.
Media matters
North Korea routinely punishes citizens for watching foreign media or listening to foreign music which is typically smuggled into the country and distributed on thumb drives and easily concealable micro SD cards.
Distributing it can result in the death penalty . In one high profile case reported in 2021 by RFA, a man was sentenced to death for selling copies of the hit Netflix series “Squid Game.”
This image courtesy of Netflix shows a scene from South Korea's "Squid Game" season one.
(Youngkyu Park/Netflix via AFP) Offenders that merely watched foreign media – but did not distribute it – are usually given a lesser, but still harsh sentence in a labor camp. Parents can even be punished for the crimes of their children. Citizens can even be presumed guilty on tangential evidence – speaking like South Koreans or texting using South Korean spellings – habits they are presumed to have picked up from watching illegal videos from the South.
Despite the government’s efforts, including the passage in 2020 of the draconian Elimination of Reactionary Thought and Culture Law, which lays out specific punishments for foreign media-related crimes, North Koreans continue to tune in.
But members of the military are under even more scrutiny. A task force called the “109 Group” catches soldiers with surprise inspections, and after a soldier is caught , reports of punishments soon follow.
Because every North Korean spends seven to 10 years in the military after high school, the appetite for South Korean and U.S. media among soldiers is quite high, Yoshihiro Makino, a diplomatic correspondent for the Asahi Shimbun newspaper in Japan and a visiting professor at Hiroshima University, told RFA.
“With so many young people gathered in one organization, it is impossible to say that none of them are interested in that kind of culture,” Makino said.
Footage of a North Korean educational propaganda video shows a soldier arrested for watching illegal foreign media.
(RFA Korean) He added that it is not common in North Korea to see public accounts of military trials, because of the need to protect military secrets, so the fact that the proceedings are shown in the educational video indicates that authorities are concerned about the spread of South Korean culture, which they refer to as ideological contamination.
“Puppet-trash culture”
The educational video continues by showing several people in courtrooms being cuffed and led away as the narrator chastises foreign media watchers for being infected by the culture of the “puppets” of the United States – an oft-used pejorative referring to South Koreans. She calls these people “weeds of our society” and “trash of our era.”
She then blames the U.S. and South Korea for spreading “rotten capitalist and puppet-trash culture on a massive scale,” and complains about sanctions aimed at depriving Pyongyang of cash and resources that could be funneled into its nuclear and missile programs, calling them a U.S. “strangulation campaign.”
Against this backdrop she asks if watching foreign media could be anything but treason.
“Are not those infected by the political poison spread by the enemy a band of traitors acting as one with our principal enemies, and poisonous mushrooms that must be uprooted entirely?”
The narrator goes on to remind soldiers that they aren’t supposed to use civilian mobile phones, with the video showing examples of smartphones and flip phones that authorities confiscated.
Footage of a North Korean educational propaganda video shows mobile phones confiscated from soldiers.
(RFA Korean) “Soldiers performing individual duties, including drivers of passenger vehicles, purchased, watched, stored and distributed impure recordings through civilian mobile phones,” the narrator says. “In the end, these phones led them down the path of treason and counterrevolution, ruining their lives.”
A second video file obtained by RFA, containing footage of a later section of the educational video, discusses the case of Kim Kye Hyang, a military doctor punished for watching foreign media.
“The Party educated … and even appointed her as a military doctor in the revolutionary army,” an on-camera military official says. “But look at what happened. Watching impure recordings turned her, at the very beginning of her life, into an ungrateful and contemptible person.”
Footage of a North Korean educational propaganda video shows an “arrest warrant” for Kim Kye Hyang, a military doctor who watched illegal foreign media.
(RFA Korean) The official says her parents are now devastated and they cry often, wishing she had never been born. She denounces foreign recordings as a poison that wastes time, damages health and ruins the lives of offenders and their families.
The footage then shows a detained soldier writing a confession. Weeping, he says that watching foreign recordings “once or twice” gradually filled his mind with South Korean speech patterns and capitalist ideology.
“I deeply regret it,” he says while seemingly crying. With ominous music, the line is repeated several times with an eerie echo effect over a stopped frame of his anguished face.
A female soldier, clad in pink formal wear, appears next. She identifies the regretful soldier as Ju Chol Bom and says his case is proof that watching foreign media is “the path to ruining one’s life.”
The narrator also warns that such crimes are committed through personal connections and will eventually be exposed. The message appears to be that even if authorities do not detect an offense immediately, offenders can still be caught.
“Why do people realize the value of something precious only after losing it?” the speaker asks. “Ju Chol Bom’s fate clearly demonstrates that watching the enemy’s subversive footage, while knowing it is an act of treason and rebellion that dances to the enemy’s tune, is the very path to becoming the most foolish suicide victim in the world and ruining one’s own destiny.”
A male soldier then says that the offense deserves severe punishment and suggests that offenders not only harmed themselves, but others as well.
Footage of a North Korean educational propaganda video shows a North Korean soldier reading an arrest warrant in front of a soldier who was caught illegally watching foreign media.
(RFA Korean) “Ju Chol Bom and several other offenders received sentences of five or more years of hard labor,” the male soldier says. “Because watching impure recordings is a serious crime, even a general amnesty is not permitted. In the end, with their own hands, they gouged out their own eyes.”
The loud, overarticulate voice of the narrator continues, implying that the actions of Ju and those like him dragged down others.
“But their eyes are not the only ones gouged out …”
The footage of the video abruptly cuts out.
Edited in Korean by Yi Yongin and in English by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Commentary: The story China wants you to swallow
articles.excerpt: China is marketing fish from Xinjiang as a triumph of technology and frontier development.
articles.fullText:
On May 22, 2018, China Central Television broadcast a glowing segment about salmon farming in western China. Over images of sleek fish cutting through clear water, the narrator marveled that “a precious fish like salmon, which typically lives in the open ocean,” could now be raised in the desert. Technology had made the improbable possible. “The land is the same land, and the people are the same people,” the program declared, “but when technology is brought in, miracles are born.”
Viewers were unconvinced and immediately began voicing skepticism about seafood coming from such a surprising place. Within days, Chinese social-media users questioned whether the fish on screen was actually salmon at all. “People expect Atlantic salmon, but we’re getting freshwater rainbow trout that costs half as much,” one Beijing-based WeChat account complained. “How could you not be angry?” The science writer Fang Shimin put it bluntly: “This is cheap rainbow trout being passed off as expensive salmon.”
Where the media campaign had hoped to tell a bigger and more hopeful story about the success of farming in a place most people thought was impossible, the public reaction veered in a different direction. China has rapidly expanded its fish farms in its historically restive and inland west—erecting more than 1,000 in Tibet and Xinjiang—motivated by a slate of priorities including food security, settling a nomadic and politically volatile population, poverty alleviation, and reducing fishing pressure on its polluted eastern shores.
The state-led media campaign around China’s desert seafood also sought to redirect Western attention away from human rights abuses that are pervasive in these two Chinese regions. The growth of these farms in China’s west is the focus of a sweeping investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project , a news organization in Washington, DC, which showed how much seafood from Xinjiang is reaching the U.S., including government facilities, in violation of the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act.
The backlash over rainbow trout was not only about unfair prices, but also about questions of food safety. In a 2018 interview with China Daily, food safety expert Zhong Kai reacted to Chinese companies advertising salmon that was actually trout. He advised that eating freshwater trout raw, as one would eat salmon, could lead to serious illness.
China’s aquaculture industry has expanded at staggering speed, and with that expansion have come the familiar pressures of industrial animal farming: crowding, disease, waste, and chemical intervention. Chinese researchers have increasingly found illegal quantities of drugs in farmed fish, including antibiotics and sedatives at levels that threaten humans.
Workers package farmed fish at Tianyun’s processing facility, Xinjiang Zungui Fresh Food Technology in Urumqi, Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.
(Xinjiang Tianyun Organic Agriculture via The Outlaw Ocean Project) These food safety questions are relevant outside of China. One company, called Xinjiang Tianyun Organic Agriculture, now ships to 14 countries, including the U.S., where its products are sold at Walmart and served at American schools, prisons, and military bases. This trade occurs in violation of a U.S. ban on goods produced in Xinjiang or by ethnic minorities from the region, which Congress enacted in 2021 after finding human rights abuses to be pervasive and severe there. Tianyun’s seafood reaches the U.S. by way of supplier deals with Aqua Star and Sysco, according to Bait to Plate , an online tool that tracks the fishing and seafood industries.
Tianyun said in a statement that claims of systemic forced labor “are completely factually unfounded” and described the U.S. ban as unreasonable and politically motivated. The company added that it strictly abides by China’s laws on labor and contracts. Aqua Star did not reply to a request for comment. Walmart confirmed that it sources seafood from Aqua Star. Sysco said it expects its suppliers to follow all U.S., international, and local laws and that they suspend contracts when they do not.
The Chinese efforts to promote seafood from Xinjiang are not new. As early as 2011, Vice Minister of Agriculture Niu Dun urged officials to “enhance brand building and awareness of the market expansion of Xinjiang’s seafood enterprises.” A 2017 government action plan instructed local offices to coordinate with mainstream media to “systematically publicize the progress of fishery poverty alleviation” in Xinjiang, fostering “an environment of positive public opinion.”
Workers harvesting fish at a reservoir-based aquaculture operation in Xinjiang, where salmon are raised in inland waters far from China’s coast.
(Xinjiang Tianyun via The Outlaw Ocean Project) This marketing push intensified in August 2023 when there was a sharp spike in social media posts on the topic. The hashtag “No joke—Xinjiang really does produce seafood” climbed Weibo’s Hot Search List. Videos associated with “Xinjiang seafood” amassed millions of views. Soon, the theme leapt beyond China’s own internet. YouTube, which is banned in China, saw a sharp rise in Xinjiang seafood videos that fall.
“All signs point to this being a coordinated campaign,” said Fergus Ryan, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute. He explained that it had unusual speed and reach due to top-down and algorithmic amplification, unlike natural viral events, which typically grow slowly through grassroots sharing. In his view, the campaign served to redirect attention from mounting international scrutiny after a 2023 investigation found that seafood plants in Shandong had used thousands of Xinjiang labor transfers to process fish destined for major Western markets. Against that backdrop, Ryan argued, the upbeat Xinjiang seafood videos functioned as a kind of information flooding, crowding search and recommendation systems with stories of “fishery miracles” rather than forced labor.
A Russian student named Melissa toured Tianyun’s fish farm in November 2025. Videos by “frontier influencers” are often amplified by state media outlets and state-run channels on social media.
(China Daily via The Outlaw Ocean Project) China is using other tactics to prevent companies from insulating themselves from these sorts of human rights abuses. In April 2026, the government announced new rules that would make it even more difficult for multinationals to conduct due diligence on supply chains in industries like seafood and cotton.
Part of the same effort, the Chinese government has also organized media tours for foreign reporters and actively recruited foreign food buffs—called vloggers or “frontier influencers”—to record and post videos and other testimonials about the wonders of growing fish in Xinjiang.
Among the most popular frontier influencers is a Russian student named Melissa. “Today, we’ve come to a salmon farm in Nilka, Xinjiang, to be an employee for a day and see what it’s like for ourselves,” she said in a video published in September 2025. These videos were amplified by media outlets affiliated with the government, as well as on state-run channels on YouTube and Facebook. A video featuring Jack, an American vlogger, showcased his tour of a fish farm on the edge of the desert. “It’s incredible how they have developed such a barren land to this extent,” he narrated.
At the Jilintai salmon farming area, Xinjiang, fishing team members tighten giant nets and harvest salmon using automated equipment.
(Zhao Xuelin/Xinjiang Tianyun via The Outlaw Ocean Project) But it is the government itself that attempts to frame the unlikely industry it has engineered in Xinjiang in the grandest terms. In a 2025 article published by state media, Xinjiang’s aquaculture hotbed in the deserts and rivers of its forbidding western frontier was declared “a testament to human ingenuity and resilience.”
“Xinjiang’s aquaculture is not merely about producing fish,” the article went on, “it is about reimagining how inland regions can contribute to the nation’s protein security, how technology can redefine agriculture, and how harmony between people and nature can be sustained in the most challenging of environments. From snow-fed rivers to desert oases, Xinjiang has shown that blue dreams can indeed flourish on dry land.”
This commentary is based on reporting for a larger investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project.
The Outlaw Ocean Project is a non-profit journalism organization based in Washington D.C. that produces investigative stories about human rights, labor, and environmental concerns.
The views expressed here are their own and do not reflect the position of RFA.

articles.title: Could ‘Apron Dad’ on North Korean TV pave the way for Kim Jong Un’s daughter to rule?
articles.excerpt: Experts said that normalizing a man in the kitchen could change perceptions, but society remains patriarchal.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Korean
In a scene from a North Korean TV show, a man wears a floral apron and serves a meal to his family. Analysts told Radio Free Asia that this striking reversal in gender roles could be a propaganda effort to get the people to accept North Korean leader Kim Jong Un’s daughter Ju Ae as his successor.
But the analysts noted that North Korea is still a society with rigid gender roles and warned against interpreting the scene in a way that suggests that authorities are using media to promote equality for the average North Korean woman.
‘에이 ... 설마’ 하고 찾아봤는데
진짜로 북한 드라마에 식탁 차리는 아버지 나옴 https://t.co/lvgEKWtFt3 pic.twitter.com/qVr318rBIK
— 안유명한 (@famousuomaf) September 24, 2026
Video of the scene went viral among Korean speaking users on the social media platform X as part of a larger discussion that speculated North Korea would begin slowly rolling back gender inequality and expanding women’s rights to prepare for Ju Ae’s ascension. The first post in the discussion was viewed 4.3 million times.
Though North Korea has made no official announcement regarding a successor, South Korea’s spy agency told lawmakers Sept. 1 that Kim Ju Ae appears to have reached the “ designated successor ” stage.
One user in the online conversation said that North Korean TV shows were already preparing the people by showing working moms and dads preparing meals.
Another user posted the video of a scene – from the show “A New Spring in the Plains of Baekhak” – that shows the aproned man with a tray full of food, entering the room from the kitchen. His wife thanks him for his effort and assists him with untying the apron strings as he places the food on the table. This post was viewed 2.4 million times.
When asked if TV shows could be part of preliminary work to establish Kim Ju Ae’s succession, Yoshihiro Makino, a foreign affairs specialist for Japan’s Asahi Shimbun newspaper and a visiting professor at Hiroshima University, told RFA that it was possible.
“In North Korea, TV is not entertainment but an important means of political propaganda,” he said. But this would be “a measure solely for Kim Ju Ae,” not for an ordinary woman.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, front right, his daughter Ju Ae, and other soldiers on a tank at a military training base in North Korea, on March 19, 2026.
(KCNA via KNS/AP) Connecting the scene to succession plans might be a bit of a stretch, because scenes showing men cooking or serving food to the family are not totally new, Rachel Minyoung Lee, a senior researcher at the Washington-based Stimson Center, who analyzes North Korean state media, told RFA.
“North Korean TV has started showing such scenes since at least the mid-2010s,” she said. “We tend to link them to succession these days because of Kim Ju Ae … I think it would be premature to jump to link this to succession.”
Whether the scene is an effort by authorities to normalize men participating more in domestic chores is unknown, but even if it is, very few North Koreans would be swayed, Kim Su Kyong, a North Korean escapee from the northeastern coastal port city of Chongjin, who now resides in Virginia, told RFA.
“Just because a man sets the table in a drama, there is no way residents will be moved by it or their perception will change toward men helping with housework,” she said.
The patriarchy still exists
North Koreans might resist Kim Ju Ae as the ruler of the country because male chauvinism permeates every aspect of society, said Kim the escapee.
“If Kim Jong Un’s daughter were to take on the role … they would really hate it,” she said. “Inside, they would be truly annoyed, but they would have to hold it in because they would be afraid that people watching will snitch on them, and they’d be punished.”
The North Korean leadership does have women in prominent roles, but these women were usually born into privilege, said Lee.
Kim Jong Un’s sister Kim Yo Jong, who was at one time widely considered to be next in line , is currently director of the ruling Korean Workers’ Party’s General Affairs Department. Meanwhile North Korea’s female foreign minister, Choe Son Hui, is the daughter of a former North Korean premier.
“These are people… who have special status right?” said Lee. “And just because you see some of these high-level females playing a role, an important role in the North Korean leadership system, I don’t think that automatically translates into a higher status for North Korean women at large.”
Lee added that even among the privileged class, men still have an overwhelming advantage. “If you look at the overall North Korean leadership chart, where you have all of the high-level North Korean officials laid out. They’re mostly men.”
An assistant shows a woman a jacket during the opening of the 2023-Autumn Garment Exhibition at the Okryu Exhibition House in Pyongyang on Nov. 9, 2023.
(Kim Won Jin/AFP) The status of ordinary women remains very low, Makino said. “According to those who have visited North Korea, many women work in hospitals and schools, but only men hold positions of responsibility.”
Over the years, the relative economic power of women has increased due to the emergence of North Korea’s nascent market economy, the Seoul-based Korea Institute for National Unification said in its 2025 North Korean Human Rights White Paper. But the study noted women still were not equal in politics and the public sphere.
Messaging from North Korean authorities regarding gender equality has also been somewhat contradictory.
On the occasion of the 80th anniversary of national founder Kim Il Sung’s July 30, 1946 decree on gender equality, the state-run Rodong Sinmun newspaper ran a story proclaiming that North Korean women have participated in the revolution with equal rights alongside men for 80 years.
But two weeks earlier, the founder’s grandson, the current leader Kim Jong Un met with newly elected leaders of the Socialist Women’s Union, where he emphasized the role of women as nurturing mothers.
“Women must become true patriots who genuinely contribute to the flourishing prosperity of the motherland, communist mothers who raise their children well, and communist educators,” he said.
The mixture between North Korea’s male-dominated culture and political ideology is responsible for the contradiction, said Lee.
“Culturally, they’re very conservative and patriarchal,” she said. “But …ideology wise because they claim themselves to be a socialist state, they’ve always emphasized gender equality."
Edited by Noh Jung Min in Korean and Eugene Whong in English.

articles.title: From a cardboard box to an iron cage: a father’s fight for his daughter’s freedom
articles.excerpt: A Uyghur father took in an abandoned Chinese baby. 40 years later he pleads for her release from a Chinese prison.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Uyghur
In 1986, a Uyghur kebab vendor found a Chinese baby in a cardboard box on his way home from work. Now Abdulla Tomur is willing to do anything to get Zohregul – the abandoned girl he raised as his daughter – released from a Chinese prison.
Abdulla hasn’t been back to the Uyghur region since a year before Chinese authorities began their large-scale “anti-terrorism” Uyghur internment campaign in 2017, during which Zohregul was arrested.
From Istanbul, Turkey, where he currently resides, Abdulla tells Radio Free Asia the story of his first encounter with Zohregul, and how he now feels powerless to help his imprisoned daughter.
Cries from a cardboard box
At the time when he found Zohregul, Abdulla had been operating a market stall in Guizhou province, far away from Kucha (in Chinese, Kuche), Aksu prefecture (Akesu), his hometown in the Uyghur region. The family had relocated to southern China due to economic hardship.
One day, after packing up his kebab equipment, he started to return home, but stopped when he heard a baby crying.
The sound came from a cardboard box left in front of a hospital. He hurried toward it, finding what appeared to be an abandoned Han Chinese baby girl.
At first he was hesitant. He thought about what his wife might say. They were already struggling to support their two young sons. He imagined her asking how they could possibly feed a third child when poverty had driven them to move so far away.
He started toward home again, but the thought of the crying baby tugged at his heartstrings.
Though the baby was left in front of the hospital, Abdulla said he had reason to believe those inside already knew she had been abandoned, and because he did not speak Chinese, communicating with them would have been difficult.
So, he decided it would be easier to take the baby and hand her over to the authorities later. He lifted her from the box, wrapped her in the cloth he used to cover his kebab meat, and carried her home.
His wife’s response was nothing like the one he had feared.
Instead of scolding him, she condemned the people who had abandoned the infant.
“How could anyone leave an innocent baby like this?” she asked.
She began breastfeeding the girl. The crying subsided, and the baby fell asleep.
The couple planned to care for her for three days before taking her to the authorities. By the fourth day, they had changed their minds.
Their sons, aged three and five, were already attached to their new companion. Abdulla recalled that they put aside their toys and gathered around her.
The parents decided to keep her until she was about a year old, then hand her over to the authorities when they returned to their hometown in the Aksu area.
But by her first birthday, she was their daughter, and a sister to their sons.
“How could we hand over a child who called us ‘Dad’ and ‘Mom’?” Abdulla said.
The family secret
Eventually the family returned to the Uyghur region.
Zohregul grew up in Kucha, in a Uyghur household, as a native speaker of the Uyghur language, and a follower of the Muslim religion – an upbringing firmly anchored in Uyghur culture.
They did not disclose Zohregul’s background to the authorities at the time because they wanted to keep it secret. Birth certificates were not required or routinely issued then, so they could register her as their own child unless someone else came forward to claim her. Late registration was also possible by paying a fine.
People suspected that his daughter was not Uyghur, but most avoided asking out of respect. Only a few close relatives asked. Abdulla told them, “She might have been switched at the hospital, but at this point, I have no way to investigate.”
Zohregul also repeatedly asked, “Why don’t I look like my two brothers?” He would reply, “You look like my grandmother.”
The family’s remaining concern was how people in their community might react if they learned Zohregul was Han Chinese.
Abdulla feared that his neighbors, who considered the Chinese presence in the Uyghur homeland to be an occupation , would be bothered by his family raising a Chinese child.
He had already formulated a response – rooted in his Muslim faith – should anyone confront the family over their decision.
“Our religion teaches that every child is born innocent,” he said. “This child is pure and innocent. Her blood relationship to those who oppress us was not her choice. She is one of God’s servants.”
Still, he doubted that this explanation would satisfy everyone, so he and his wife decided to keep Zohregul’s origins a family secret.
A family divided
In 2016, Abdulla traveled to Turkey to visit his eldest son, who was studying in Istanbul. When the mass arrests by the Chinese government under the “Strike Hard Campaign Against Violent Terrorism” intensified the next year in the Uyghur region, he wanted to return home. Abdulla had already been sent to a camp the year before for “illegal gathering.” He said that while incarcerated , he was deprived of sleep and forced to confess to alleged illegal activities by himself or his neighbors.
But Abdulla’s son urged him to stay, fearing that his father too would be detained again. From Istanbul, Abdulla worried constantly about his children at home, especially Zohregul. He had nightmares of seeing her in handcuffs.
Eventually, an acquaintance told Abdulla that both Zohregul and his younger son Rehim were in prison. As with many other detentions by Chinese authorities at the time, no official reason was given.
Upon hearing this, a father’s first impulse was to return home immediately. But Abdulla realized he would be unable to help either child if he returned and became imprisoned himself.
At first, he convinced himself that the detentions could not continue indefinitely.
“How could they keep so many people for so long?” he recalled thinking. “Surely they would release them.”
Revealing the truth
In 2020, three years after learning about his children’s detentions, Abdulla – still in Turkey – began trying to secure their release. He participated in demonstrations outside the Chinese Consulate in Istanbul, appearing in media interviews, and trying to find more information.
When six years of those efforts yielded no results, he took to social media and made a direct appeal to Chinese authorities.
“I am an uneducated farmer,” he said. “I have not participated in political activities here. Please give me information about my children. If they are in prison, release them.”
He offered to return to the Uyghur region to resume farming, or submit to imprisonment himself.
“At least release my innocent daughter, Zohregul,” he pleaded.
Abdulla said the appeal circulated on Facebook and then on Douyin – the Chinese version of TikTok – where it received more than 50,000 views.
Four people contacted him, claiming to be consular personnel, customs officers, or police.
They said they would help, but the conversations soon turned to requests for information about Uyghurs in Syria and Afghanistan. Abdulla said he knew nothing and could not provide them with any information.
During one conversation, out of desperation, he disclosed that Zohregul was an adopted Han Chinese child and asked the caller to relay that information to officials in Aksu.
It was the first time Abdulla had publicly revealed his daughter’s Chinese origin, in the hope of getting help to secure her release from prison.
Abdulla hoped her ancestry might make a difference. During his years in Kucha, he had seen officials pay particular attention to Chinese settlers’ safety. He also recalled authorities rewarding Uyghur families who adopted Chinese children as part of “ethnic unity” campaigns.
One Chinese officer showed interest after learning the family secret, Abdulla said. But the officer only told him that Zohregul had received a 12-year sentence and had three years remaining.
The officer also told him to return to China and “repent” before they could discuss his daughter’s situation further.
An RFA investigation in September 2026 determined that the officer who told Abdulla about his daughter’s imprisonment worked in Kucha’s Ogen (Weigan) township. A different police officer in Kucha’s Alaqagha (Alahage) township separately confirmed to RFA that two members of Abdulla’s family were imprisoned, including Zohregul.
RFA was also able to get official confirmation why Zohregul was punished. It was because her father had traveled to Turkey, which Beijing considers to be a “sensitive country” and because she read “illegal” religious materials.
China maintains excessive travel restrictions for Uyghurs, bans religious materials — even those previously approved by the government — and punishes family members through a policy of guilt by association.
A family tragedy
Zohregul has now been imprisoned for nine years.
Given his own brief detention by the Chinese authorities, Abdulla worries about how she could endure interrogation, mistreatment and the restrictions of confinement, although the available information does not confirm her current conditions.
He said he was caught between the urge to return and the fear that doing so would put another member of the family behind bars.
Abdulla is currently on a pilgrimage to Mecca, and before leaving, he said he would carry those fears in his prayers.
The abandoned baby he once lifted from a roadside box is still his daughter, he said. But the compassion that enabled him to bring her home in 1986 cannot open her prison door.
“O Allah, I had the strength to rescue Zohregul from a cardboard box,” he said, explaining what he says when he prays. “But I do not have the strength to rescue her from an iron cage. Forgive me. Forgive my sins.”
Translated by Shohret Hoshur. Edited by Eugene Whong and Charlie Dharapak.

articles.title: Human resources meeting held
articles.excerpt: Chief Secretary Chan Kwok-ki today chaired the seventh meeting of the fourth-term Human Resources Planning Commission, with members acknowledging that the youth unemployment situation warrants attention. The meeting heard that rising unemployment and the youth employment…
articles.fullText:
Chief Secretary Chan Kwok-ki today chaired the seventh meeting of the fourth-term Human Resources Planning Commission, with members acknowledging that the youth unemployment situation warrants attention.

The meeting heard that rising unemployment and the youth employment situation are structural challenges faced by most advanced economies worldwide, Hong Kong being no exception.

Members took note that the Government continues to invest heavily in education and skills training for the local workforce. This includes launching a two-year 30,000 Youth Employment & Internship Programme, as announced in the Policy Address, to facilitate youth employment and development.

The Labour Department will also launch the Youth Employment Link online service portal to facilitate young people's access to employment information and support services. Looking ahead, the continued expansion of the local economy is expected to underpin overall labour market conditions.

The Labour & Welfare Bureau also briefed the meeting on the "Mid-term Update of Manpower Projection" report. Members heard that the Government will continue to promote "AI for All" and support lifelong learning, ensuring that skills in the labour force remain aligned with Hong Kong's future economy.

The bureau will commence a new review of the Talent List soon.

Members said they supported the Government in continuing to closely monitor the labour market and in formulating and refining forward-looking policies on a rolling basis, with a view to maintaining manpower supply in support of economic development, whilst also safeguarding employment priority for local workers.

articles.title: Myanmar junta airstrikes target civilians to coerce Arakan Army into peace talks
articles.excerpt: Rakhine rebel leadership says continued bombing of civilians negates trust required for negotiations.
articles.fullText:
Myanmar’s military-backed government is increasingly resorting to attacks on civilians as a means to bring the rebel Arakan Army in the western coastal state of Rakhine to the negotiating table, Rakhine politicians and analysts told Radio Free Asia.
Airstrikes targeting civilians for peace talks
The government launched an airstrike on the town of Kyauktaw, dropping bombs on a crowded marketplace and other civilian areas killing at least 50 people, including children and pregnant women, according to the Arakan Army, or AA, an armed ethnic group which controls most of the towns in Rakhine.
The U.N. Human Rights Office released a statement noting that this attack was one of the deadliest airstrikes in Rakhine State since the military took control of the country in a coup in 2021. Fortify Rights Friday released a statement saying that the attack could constitute a war crime.
Several other ethnic groups, some of whom had been allied with and fought alongside the AA after the coup, have begun participating in peace talks over the past few months. The AA is one of several major holdouts nationwide, including the Kachin Independence Army and the Karen National Union.
The attacks on civilians are one of several tactics by the military meant to force the AA into making peace, Sai Kyi Zin Soe, a Myanmar security analyst, told RFA.
“One side has laid out the path it wants. But they are using various forms of coercion to pressure the other side to reach that intended path,” he said. “This includes military force. There are also efforts to apply political and economic pressure in coordination with neighboring countries. You can, in other words, say this part of the military’s tactics.”
He said that attacks causing mass civilian fatalities, like the Kyauktaw attack, may also be intended to intimidate civilians to discourage them from accepting AA authority.
Violence for peace?
The attack only justified the fight against the military, Khaing Thu Kha, a spokesperson for the AA told RFA after the attack on Monday.
“We will continue to seek justice for those we’ve lost in this violent attack by identifying anyone involved in the act and taking actions against them,” he said. We will retaliate against each and every one of them.”
A fire continues to burn following a military airstrike on a market and adjacent bridge in Kyauktaw, northern Rakhine state, Myanmar, Sept. 28, 2026.
(AFP) The AA reported that over a five-month period from April 21 to to September 30 the military government extended an invitation for peace talks while simultaneously killing more than 130 civilians in AA-controlled areas in airstrikes and heavy artillery attacks.
But no faction wants to accept a peace invitation while under constant attack, Zaw Wai Soe, a minister in Myanmar’s shadow National Unity Government, made up democratically elected leaders who were ousted in the coup, told RFA.
“The bombing didn’t just start now. They’ve been doing it all along. It has gotten worse in recent days,” he said. “They drop bombs despite knowing civilians are present. So who would want to meet them? It’s not just the AA, any group would feel the same way.”
Current battlegrounds
Since early this month, the AA has engaged in fierce clashes around military-controlled Sittwe, Kyaukpyu, and Manaung townships. Meanwhile, military government forces are advancing into Rakhine from Chin State, and the Magway and the Ayeyarwady regions. Residents report that airstrikes continue in AA-controlled territories.
Direct military confrontation will continue as long as armed combat persists on the ground, Thien Tun Oo, executive director of the Thayninga Institute for Strategic Studies, a pro-military think tank in Naypyidaw, told RFA.
Victim's bodies are laid out at a cemetery before their burial following a military airstrike on a market and adjacent bridge in Kyauktaw, northern Rakhine state, Myanmar, on Sept. 28, 2026.
(AFP) “We will hold discussions for peace. However, for those who continue to rely on military means on the ground, they will naturally face head-on military confrontations,” he said. “Those relying heavily on military force will encounter military responses.”
RFA attempted to contact Brig. Gen. San Nyo Win, military spokesperson for Rakhine state, for comment on the situation, but phone calls went unanswered.
The airstrikes make it more difficult for the AA to accept an invitation to peace talks, Thar Tun Hla, chairman of the Arakan National Party, which represents the interests of Rakhine nationalists, told RFA.
“The peace process requires trust,” he said. “Firing on civilian targets cannot be viewed as a trust-building process.”
Translated by Kyaw Min Htun. Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Students share Beijing learnings
articles.excerpt: The Education Bureau held the learning outcomes sharing session of the "Salute to the National Flag" Beijing Visit Delegation at Kowloon Technical School today, promoting the outcomes of the activity among more young people and various sectors of the society. About 250 student…
articles.fullText:
The Education Bureau held the learning outcomes sharing session of the "Salute to the National Flag" Beijing Visit Delegation at Kowloon Technical School today, promoting the outcomes of the activity among more young people and various sectors of the society.

About 250 student representatives of the delegation from tertiary institutions, secondary and primary schools shared their learning experiences during the five-day visit to Beijing.

Speaking at the session, Chief Secretary Chan Kwok-ki described the delegation as a high-level "walking classroom", which enabled students to feel for themselves the national dignity represented by the national flag and the national anthem through the solemn flag-raising ceremony at Tiananmen Square.

He said that this deepened their understanding of the symbolic meaning of the national flag, and strengthened their sense of national identity and patriotism.

Mr Chan said that students experienced at first hand our country's journey from arduous struggle to the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation from the country's millennia-old cultural heritage to the development achievements of the new era.

He added that the delegation was received in person by Member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and Vice Premier of the State Council Ding Xuexiang, and by the Director of the Hong Kong and Macao Work Office of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office of the State Council Xia Baolong at the Great Hall of the People.

“Mr Ding conveyed the cordial remarks and exhortations of President Xi and the Central Government to the young people from Hong Kong and Macao, enabling students to feel the care and expectations of the Central Authorities for Hong Kong and Macao young people, and to understand more deeply the important meaning carried by the national flag,” Mr Chan said.

He emphasised that patriotic education has all along been a top priority of the work of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region Government. Hong Kong's First Five-Year Plan and the 2026 Policy Address also list the promotion of patriotic education as a key task.

He noted that today's learning outcomes sharing session aims to pass on more widely and further what the students learned in Beijing, so that more young people may gain a deeper understanding of the important meaning of the national flag and feel more deeply our country's care and concern for young people.

He said the Government will continue to join hands with various sectors of the society and, through rich and diverse means, enable young people to build a firm sense of national identity, national confidence and a sense of responsibility through first-hand experience.

Today's sharing session began with a flag-raising ceremony. A joint team formed by flag-raising teams of the Association of Hong Kong Flag-guards and the Hong Kong Army Cadets Association, drawing on the experience of exchanges and interaction in Beijing with the People's Liberation Army Ceremonial Escort Battalion, conducted a solemn flag-raising ceremony. Booths were also set up at the session for members of the delegation to introduce their learning experience in Beijing.

Around 1,200 flag-raising team representatives, teachers, students and youth group representatives from Hong Kong and Macao joined the delegation’s thematic activity in Beijing from September 18 to 22.

articles.title: Domestic helper wage up 2.35%
